Special-status Plants Big tarplant (Blepharizonia plumosa) has a California Rare Plant Rank (CRPR) of 1B.1, indicating that this species is rare, threatened, or endangered in California and elsewhere, and is seriously threatened in California (over 80 percent of occurrences threatened). This species can be found in valley grassland habitats. Big tarplant was found on the western portion of the Project site during rare plant surveys (Tetra Tech 2022b). Two populations of big tarplant were observed within the Project site, both of which occur in Alameda County (Figure 4.4-2); population 1 consisted of 395 individuals (0.09 acre), and population 2 consisted of 167 individuals (0.15 acre). Both populations occurred in ephemeral erosional features that had higher cover of bare soil relative to other areas of the Project site (Tetra Tech 2022b). California Tiger Salamander CTS is a federally and state threatened species. Ephemeral ponds lasting at least 30 days for breeding and an additional 10 weeks for larval development are necessary for successful breeding (USFWS 2004). Suitable breeding habitat consists of vernal pools, stock ponds, or other ephemeral wetlands that do not contain fish or bullfrog predators. Emergent or submerged vegetation or debris is necessary for egg attachment. Suitable upland habitat includes grazed annual grassland no further than 1.24 miles from a known or potential breeding site (USFWS 2003). Networks of small mammal burrows in upland habitat are necessary for CTS estivation (i.e., dormancy during hot, dry season) (Pittman 2005). The Project site has many California ground squirrel burrows in San Joaquin and Alameda Counties (all except two are in San Joaquin County) as shown in Figure 4.4-3. In addition, an ephemeral pond in the southeast portion of the Project site was observed in 2023 after a historically high rainfall year. This pond could provide CTS breeding habitat, however the presence of cattle and their trampling around the pond may reduce the likelihood of it being used 4 Environmental Analysis 4.4 Biological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.4-10 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 for breeding purposes. Therefore, the Project site is potential upland and breeding habitat and may support estivating and breeding amphibians. One concrete cattle trough was found on-site, but is unlikely to be used as CTS breeding habitat because there was no bank or slope for CTS to access the water in the trough, and CTS cannot climb over structures greater than 15 inches (Langton 2021). An assessment was also conducted within 1.24 miles of the Project site to analyze potential barriers to CTS migration between potential breeding ponds/pools and the Project site (Figure 4.4-4). The nearest known breeding site is 2 miles to the southwest of the Project site (CDFW 2022). Within 1.24 miles, five potential breeding pools exist (Pool Numbers 1 through 5 in Figure 4.4-4); two pools were visited and determined to be potential CTS breeding pools (Pool Numbers 1 and 5) and three potential breeding habitats (Pool Numbers 2 through 4) could not be observed because they occur on private property. The five other pools (Pool Numbers 6 through 10) shown in Figure 4.4-4 were visited in the field and determined to not be potential breeding habitat for CTS (Tetra Tech 2022a; USFWS 2003). Two types of potential CTS barriers were identified within 1.24 miles of the Project site: high-density development and steep slopes over 14 degrees without passages. Migration from Pool Number 1 is affected by one partial barrier (PG&E Tesla Substation), dispersal from Pool 2 is affected by one partial barrier (Union Pacific Railroad), and Pools 3 and 4 have no barriers to CTS migration as shown in Figure 4.4-4. Based on this assessment, CTS could migrate through the Project site. California Red-legged Frog CRLF is a federally threatened species and a CDFW Species of Special Concern. Ideal CRLF breeding habitat has emergent vegetation and surface water at a 2-foot depth or deeper; water must last a minimum of 4 to 6 months for breeding and metamorphosis. This species is also known to use stock ponds and cattle troughs for breeding (Hemingway 2005). Ideal upland habitats are creeks, seeps, or freshwater spring corridors with riparian vegetation, but this species can also occupy other types of upland habitats, including annual grassland. CRLF upland habitat is typically located within 1 mile of a breeding site. The Project site provides potential CRLF estivation habitat primarily in the form of California ground squirrel burrows. CRLF may roam away from aquatic sites as much as 1 mile on rainy nights (USFWS 2005). Although the nearest known CRLF breeding pond is 1.5 miles northwest of the Project site from 2004 (CDFW 2022), two potential breeding ponds were found within 1 mile during the surveys (Pool Numbers 1 and 6 in Figure 4.4-4). In addition, there are at least seven cattle ponds approximately 1.5 miles to the west and southwest of the Project site, as well as four ephemeral creeks within 0.5 to 1 mile that could facilitate safe dispersal for CRLF from these potential breeding sites to the Project site. The ephemeral pond in the southeast of the Project site may attract CRLF dispersing across the area to be developed but is not breeding habitat due to the lack of emergent vegetation. Overall, the Project site may provide upland dispersal habitat that could be used by CRLF, but does not provide breeding habitat given the lack of suitable breeding habitat on-site. Western Spadefoot Western spadefoot is a CDFW Species of Special Concern. The spadefoot toad is primarily found in open grasslands and breeds in seasonal shallow waters such as ephemeral ponds, vernal pools, or intermittent streams. They spend most of their time in underground burrows that they 4 Environmental Analysis 4.4 Biological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.4-11 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 construct themselves, becoming active on the surface nocturnally during rains or when humidity is high (Stebbins 1972). The ephemeral pond in the southeast portion of the Project site provides potential breeding habitat for western spadefoot, when water is present. The surrounding grasslands provides potential upland dispersal habitat. Since common amphibians were observed in this pond (i.e., California toad and Sierran treefrog), this pond has the potential to support special-status amphibians. Special-Status Reptiles California glossy snake and San Joaquin coachwhip are CDFW Species of Special Concern. These reptiles inhabit grassland habitats. California glossy snake is a primarily fossorial species and is found in areas with sandy and loose soils. The San Joaquin coachwhip inhabits open, valley grassland habitats with sparse shrub cover and requires small mammal burrows for egg-laying and refuge. The Project site provides potential habitat for the California glossy snake and San Joaquin coachwhip in the form of grassland habitat (i.e., Avena spp.–Bromus spp. Herbaceous Semi-natural Alliance) with small mammal burrows. Special-status Vernal Pool Invertebrates Special-status vernal pool invertebrates have an ephemeral lifecycle, relying on seasonal ponds formed during winter rains. These vernal pools or seasonal ponds have an impervious substrate layer that allow for water to pond. Cysts from the substrate hatch when pools fill with rainwater and then rapidly develop into adults. When the pools dry, offspring persist as desiccation-resistant cysts in the pond soil until the return of winter rains the following year. The ephemeral pond in the southeast portion of the Project site may provide habitat for special-status vernal pool invertebrate species. The federally endangered longhorn fairy shrimp (Branchinecta longiantenna) and federally threatened vernal pool fairy shrimp (Branchinecta lynchi) are documented to occur more than 5 miles away north and west of the Project site (CDFW 2022). Since the Project site is within the known range of these species and due to the presence of suitable ponding habitat, special-status vernal pool invertebrates may occur within the ephemeral pond. However, based on a review of available aerial imagery from 1937 to 2022, this pond only holds water seasonally during high rainfall years and is typically dry. Crotch’s Bumble Bee Crotch’s bumble bee is a candidate for listing under the California Endangered Species Act (CESA). Crotch’s bumble bee primarily nest in late February through late October in abandoned small mammal burrows underground. Overwintering sites include soft, disturbed soil or leaf litter or other debris used by mated queens. Crotch’s bumble bee forages a variety of suitable floral resources, including plants in the Asteraceae, Boraginaceae, Fabaceae, and Hydrophyllaceae families (Xerces Society et al. 2018). Although no bumble bees of any species were observed during Project biological surveys and there are no known occurrences recorded near the Project site, floral resources (foraging habitat), burrows and crevices (nesting habitat), and leaf litter (overwintering habitat) were observed within the Project site. However, the site is routinely grazed and trampled by cattle, which likely interferes 4 Environmental Analysis 4.4 Biological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.4-12 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 with the habitat requirements of this species and reduces habitat suitability (Xerces Society et al. 2018). Burrowing Owl BUOW is a CDFW Species of Special Concern. BUOWs breed and live in burrows and use coastal prairie, coastal scrub, Great Basin grassland, Great Basin scrub, Mojavean Desert scrub, Sonoran Desert scrub, and valley and foothill grassland habitats as well as agricultural areas or any open dry area with low vegetation. The Project site is in the known distributional range of the BUOW and contains potentially suitable BUOW habitat due to low-growing vegetation and abundance of small mammals. In addition, this species has been previously documented on the Project site in 2007 (CDFW 2022). A total of eight small mammal burrows and one burrow surrogate (i.e., culvert) that were potentially suitable for BUOW were found within the Project site in San Joaquin and Alameda Counties (all except one are in San Joaquin County) as shown in Figure 4.4-3. These burrows had entrance diameters greater than approximately 4 inches and were above 60 inches in depth and, therefore, were considered potentially suitable for BUOW (Tetra Tech 2022a). Although no BUOW sign was observed at the potential burrows or burrow surrogate, several burrow networks that could support BUOW were found on-site. Swainson’s Hawk Swainson’s hawk is a state threatened species, and the San Joaquin Valley hosts the majority of California’s breeding pairs. This species nests primarily in riparian or isolated trees between March and September. Potential Swainson’s hawk and raptor nesting habitat within 0.5 mile of the Project site consists of more than 10 transmission towers and numerous 8- to 10-foot-tall trees of various species in residential areas and in stands along ephemeral water features in San Joaquin and Alameda Counties (Figure 4.4-5). Although trees within the BSA are considered potential Swainson’s hawk habitat, these residential areas are exposed to high levels of disturbance (e.g., vehicle traffic, dogs, human activity, noise, light pollution). Adjacent areas in the 0.5-mile buffer undergo comparably less disturbance. One inactive raptor nest was found in a transmission tower approximately 100 feet east from the Project site in San Joaquin County (Figure 4.4-5). Overall, Swainson’s hawk could use the Project site as foraging habitat, but there is a low potential for this species to nest on-site since the only trees occur in residential areas. This species could nest within 0.5 mile of the Project site. White-tailed Kite The white-tailed kite is a fully protected species by CDFW. White-tailed kites forage for rodents and insects in undisturbed grasslands, meadows, farmlands, and emergent wetlands (Thompson 1975). Their nesting habitat includes dense oak, willow, or other tree stand, usually 6 to 20 meters above ground, located near an open foraging area (Dixon et al. 1957). Nesting typically occurs from March through early August, peaking from March through June. Potential white-tailed kite nesting habitat includes trees located adjacent to the Project site to the north and northwest. Numerous 8- to 10-foot-tall trees of various species in residential areas have 4 Environmental Analysis 4.4 Biological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.4-13 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 the potential to provide nesting habitat. The open grassland within the Project site provides potential foraging habitat for white-tailed kites. This species uses grasslands and sparsely vegetated shrubland habitats. SJKF digs and lives in dens and preys primarily on small mammals, but may also feed on various insects, reptiles, birds and eggs, and rarely vegetation. Suitable SJKF dens are defined as any suitable underground hole that has entrances of 5 to 8 inches in diameter, including those of other species and manmade features that meet the size requirement (USFWS 2011). The Project site supports an abundant prey base and friable soils for burrows/dens. SJKF have been previously documented on the Project site in 1989, and there are 10 occurrences within 5 miles of the Project site from before 2000 (CDFW 2022). Long-term surveys beginning in 2016 and continuing for 10 years to 2026 on the Contra Costa Water District’s 3,000-acre Corral Hollow property just southeast of the Project site are being performed. When native vegetation is cleared, fragmented patches of open space or isolated “islands” of wildlife habitat are created. Fragmentation and habitat loss are the two main contributors to continuing biodiversity decline. The main goal of corridors is to facilitate movement of individuals through dispersal, seasonal migration, and movement for foraging, breeding, cover, etc. Corridors allow for physical and genetic exchange between isolated wildlife populations and are critical for the maintenance of ecological processes, including allowing for the movement of animals and the continuation of viable populations and higher species diversity. The Project site lies within an area designated as Rank 4 in CDFW’s Terrestrial Connectivity Areas of Conservation Emphasis. This designation indicates that habitat connectivity linkages occur in the area. Habitat connectivity linkages represent the best connections between core natural areas to maintain habitat connectivity. However, these linkages are not considered irreplaceable and essential corridors (i.e., Rank 5). The Project site is also within the California Bay Area Linkage Network (Penrod et al. 2013), which identifies areas that are either high-quality habitat or highly permeable to wildlife movement and connect larger wildlands with smaller wildlands. In addition, the Project site is within a San Joaquin Valley Wildlife Corridor (Huber 2006). San Joaquin Valley Wildlife Corridors connect areas of conservation opportunity to healthy, native habitats. However, these designated areas also extend far beyond the boundaries of the Project site and have not incorporated specific on-site conditions into the analysis. 4 Environmental Analysis 4.4 Biological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.4-20 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 The residential and heavy grazing uses and lack of natural habitat on the Project site, as well as grazing and development of the surrounding areas, may limit habitat continuity or wildlife movement on-site. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Fisheries share responsibility for administration of the ESA. These responsibilities include listing and delisting species, designating critical habitat, and formulating recovery plans. The USFWS has primary responsibility for terrestrial and freshwater organisms, while the responsibilities of NOAA Fisheries are mainly marine wildlife. The ESA is divided into 18 sections that are intended to work together to prevent species from going extinct by helping to stabilize populations, reducing the threats to their survival, and helping species recover to the point that they no longer require federal protection. Once a species is listed, Section 9 of the Endangered Species Act makes it unlawful for any person, including private and public entities, to “take” species listed as endangered without a permit issued under Section 10 or an incidental take statement issued under Section 7. “Incidental take” is defined as take that is incidental to, and not the purpose of, the carrying out of an otherwise lawful activity. 4.4.2.2 Federal Migratory Bird Treaty Act The federal MBTA of 1918 (Title 16, U.S.C. §§703–712), as amended, implements various treaties and conventions between the United States and Canada, Japan, Mexico, and the former Soviet Union for the protection of migratory birds. The MBTA makes it unlawful to pursue, hunt, take, capture, kill, possess, sell, purchase, barter, import, export, or transport any migratory bird, or any part, nest, or egg or any such bird, unless authorized under a permit issued by the Secretary of the Interior. Some regulatory exceptions apply. “Take” is defined in regulations implementing the MBTA as “to pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or attempt to carry out these activities.” The MBTA prohibits the collection and destruction of a migratory bird, its nest, and birds or eggs contained in the nest. USFWS’ Migratory Bird Permit Memorandum (MBPM-2) dated April 15, 2003, clarifies that destruction of most unoccupied bird nests is permissible under the MBTA; exceptions include nests of federally listed threatened or endangered migratory birds, bald eagles (Haliaeetus leucocephalus), and golden eagles. Take under the MBTA does not include habitat destruction or alteration, if there is not a direct taking of birds, nests, eggs, or parts thereof. The USFWS has statutory authority and responsibility for enforcing the MBTA. 4.4.2.3 California Endangered Species Act (Fish and Game Code §2050 et seq.) CESA was enacted in 1984 to parallel the federal ESA and allows the California Fish and Game Commission to designate species, including plants, as “threatened” or “endangered.” The CESA states that all native species of fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals, and plants, and their habitats, threatened with extinction and those experiencing a significant decline which, if not halted, would lead to a threatened or endangered designation, will be protected or preserved. In May 2022, a California Court of Appeal ruled that insects (invertebrates) can be protected under the California Endangered Species Act (see Almond Alliance of California v. California Department of Fish and Wildlife, No. C093542 [3rd District, May 31, 2022]). 4 Environmental Analysis 4.4 Biological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.4-22 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 The CESA makes it illegal to import, export, take, possess, purchase, sell, or attempt to do any of those actions to species that are designated as threatened, endangered, or candidates for listing, unless permitted by the CDFW. The objective of the CWA is “to restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation’s waters.” It establishes the basic structure for regulating discharges of pollutants into WOTUS and for regulating water quality and establishing water quality standards for surface waters. Sections 404 and 401 of the CWA are pertinent to surface and coastal WOTUS. The CWA provides regulatory authority over the navigable WOTUS, which are defined as the “waters of the United States, including the territorial seas” (33 U.S.C. §1362(7)). This statute is implemented by the USACE and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA). Congress did not define in the CWA what it meant by “Waters of the U.S.” and left it up to the USACE and USEPA to provide more detail through rulemaking. WOTUS are comprised of those wetland and non-wetland bodies of water that met criteria set forth in 33 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Section 328.3, as interpreted by several court opinions and guidance. On June 29, 2015, the USACE and USEPA published an amendment to 33 CFR Section 328.3, revising the definition of WOTUS in a manner intended to consider but supersede prior judicial decisions, regulations, and guidance. The revised regulation, named the “Clean Water Rule,” was published in the Federal Register (FR; 80 FR 124: 37054–37127) and became effective on August 28, 2015. The Clean Water Rule was challenged in court and on October 22, 2019, the USACE and USEPA published a final rule (Step One) to repeal the 2015 Clean Water Rule and to restore the regulatory text that existed prior to the 2015 Clean Water Rule. The final rule (Step One) became effective on December 23, 2019. On April 21, 2020, the USACE and USEPA completed Step Two of the two-step "repeal and replace" process by publishing The Navigable Waters Protection Rule: Definition of “Waters of the United States” in the FR. The Navigable Waters Protection Rule revises the definition of WOTUS under the CWA. It creates four categories of jurisdictional waters and it provides specific exclusions for many water features that traditionally have not been regulated. The Navigable Waters Protection Rule (Step Two) became effective on June 22, 2020, replacing the final rule (Step One). 4 Environmental Analysis 4.4 Biological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.4-24 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 Following a federal district court decision on August 30, 2021, the USACE and USEPA halted implementation of the Navigable Waters Protection Rule and began interpreting WOTUS consistent with the “pre-2015” regulatory regime. Through the Act, the California SWRCB and nine RWQCBs were entrusted with duties and powers to preserve, restore, and enhance the quality of California's water resources. The SWRCB has the ultimate authority over state water rights and water quality policy. The SWRCB adopts statewide water quality control plans, policies, and guidance that direct RWQCBs in designating beneficial uses, setting water quality control standards, and administering programs to protect and preserve the “Waters of the State.” Pursuant to these statewide plans, policies, and guidance, each of the nine RWQCBs within California is required to adopt a Basin Plan that sets water quality standards, including narrative and numeric water quality objectives for various constituents of concern, recognizing and reflecting the regional differences in existing water quality, the beneficial uses of the region’s ground and surface waters, and local water quality conditions Pursuant to Porter-Cologne, the SWRCB and RWQCBs, on a statewide and regional basis, respectively, have authority to regulate the “discharge of waste” to “Waters of the State” independently of the CWA and as a matter of state law. Discharges of waste are defined to: include sewage and any and all other waste substances, liquid, solid, gaseous, or radioactive, associated with human habitation or of human or animal origin, or from any producing, manufacturing or processing operations, include waste placed in containers of whatever nature prior to and for purposes of, disposal (California Water Code §13050(d)). Discharges of fill are included in the Porter-Cologne definition of discharge of “waste.” “Waters of the State” are defined to mean “any surface water or groundwater, including saline waters, within the boundaries of the state” (California Water Code §13050€). Under Porter-Cologne, Waters of the State include, but are not limited to, WOTUS. As a matter of state law, any party proposing a discharge of waste, including fill or other pollutants, that threatens to affect any Water of the State that is not also a WOTUS must file a Report of Waste Discharge with the appropriate RWQCB, as applicable (California Water Code §§13260; 13264). The RWQCB, after a public hearing, will then respond to the Report of Waste Discharge by imposing appropriate Waste Discharge Requirements (WDRs) (California Water Code §§13263; 13264), or by issuing a Waiver of WDRs with appropriate conditions (California Water Code §13269), to control discharges for the protection of Waters of the State. The SWRCB and RWQCBs, on a statewide and regional basis, respectively, also have authority to issue, deny, condition, enforce, and otherwise administer all CWA Section 402 NPDES Permits 4 Environmental Analysis 4.4 Biological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.4-25 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 for discharges of pollutants into WOTUS, and Section 401 water quality certifications for Section 404 permits. The Procedures define an area as a wetland as follows: an area is a wetland if, under normal circumstances: (1) the area has continuous or recurrent saturation of the upper substrate caused by groundwater, or shallow surface water, or both; (2) the duration of such saturation is sufficient to cause anaerobic conditions in the upper substrate; and (3) the area’s vegetation is dominated by hydrophytes or the area lacks vegetation. The Procedures consider natural wetlands, wetlands created by modification of surface Waters of the State, and areas that meet the current or historic definitions of WOTUS, to be Waters of the State (SWRCB 2019). In addition, the Procedures consider artificial wetlands (i.e., wetlands that result from human activity) that meet specific criteria to be Waters of the State (SWRCB 2019). The CDFW defines a “stream” (including creeks and rivers) as “a body of water that flows at least periodically or intermittently through a bed or channel having banks and supports fish or other aquatic life. This includes watercourses having surface or subsurface flow that supports or has supported riparian vegetation” (CCR, Title 14, Division 1, Subdivision 1, Chapter 1, Section 1.72). “Bank” means the slope or elevation of land that bounds the bed of the stream in a permanent or 4 Environmental Analysis 4.4 Biological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.4-26 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 longstanding way, and that confines the stream water up to its highest level. “Lake” includes “natural lakes or man-made reservoirs.” Rivers, streams, lakes, and riparian vegetation that provide habitat for fish and wildlife species are subject to jurisdiction by the CDFW under Sections 1600–1616 of the California Fish and Game Code. Riparian areas are lands adjacent to streams, lakes, and estuarine-marine shorelines. Section 2785(e) defines “riparian habitat” as lands that contain habitat which grows close to and which depends upon soil moisture from a nearby freshwater source. The CDFW regulates the bed, bank to bank, as well as associated riparian vegetation and fish and wildlife resources. The CDFW has interpreted jurisdictional boundaries to be defined by the tops of stream banks (i.e., the limit of stream influence) and/or the limit of the canopy of riparian vegetation (outer drip line) that is hydrologically connected to river, stream, or lake, whichever is greatest. As a result, the area of CDFW jurisdiction is usually greater than the active channel and overlaps and extends beyond the USACE jurisdiction. Isolated wetlands not associated with a river, stream, or lake are not protected under Sections 1600 et seq. of the California Fish and Game Code. In addition, the CDFW does not have regulatory authority on tribal lands. CDFW jurisdiction may also extend to altered or artificial waterways based upon the value of those waterways to fish and wildlife (CDFG-ESD 1994), particularly to the extent that such constructed waterways were originally natural waterways. The Lake and Streambed Alteration Program requires execution of an agreement with the CDFW before any activity substantially modifies a river, stream, or lake. It is not legal to alter the bed or bank of a stream or lake or their natural water flow without a CDFW Streambed Alteration Agreement. The California Fish and Game Code Section 1602 requires an entity to notify the CDFW of any proposed activity that may substantially modify a perennial, intermittent, and ephemeral river, stream, or lake in the state. Notification is required by any person, business, state or local government agency, or public utility that proposes an activity that will: • Substantially divert or obstruct the natural flow of any river, stream or lake; • Substantially change or use any material from the bed, channel, or bank of, any river, stream, or lake; or • Deposit or dispose of debris, waste, or other material containing crumbled, flaked, or ground pavement where it may pass into any river, stream, or lake. The notification requirement applies to any work undertaken in or near a river, stream, or lake that flows at least intermittently through a bed or channel. Impact Analysis Biological resources either may be “directly” or “indirectly” impacted by a project (defined by CEQA Guidelines section 15358): • Direct impact: impacts which are caused by the project and occur at the same time and place. Any alteration, disturbance or destruction of biological resources that could result from project-related activities is considered a direct impact. • Indirect impact: impacts which are caused by the project and are later in time or farther removed in distance but are still reasonably foreseeable. Examples include growth-inducing impacts and other impacts related to induced changes in the pattern of land use, population density, or growth rate, and related effects on air and water and other natural systems, including ecosystems. Impacts either may be “permanent” or “temporary” in nature: • Temporary impacts (short-term): impacts considered as having reversible impacts on biological resources can be viewed as temporary, such as construction noise. 4 Environmental Analysis 4.4 Biological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.4-29 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 • Permanent impacts (long-term): impacts that result in the irreversible removal of biological resources are considered permanent, such as development. 4.4.3 Thresholds of Significance A project would result in significant impacts to biological resources if it would: a) Have a substantial adverse effect, either directly or through habitat modifications, on any species identified as a candidate, sensitive, or special status species in local or regional plans, policies, or regulations, or by the California Department of Fish and Game or the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; b) Have a substantial adverse effect on any riparian habitat or other sensitive natural community identified in local or regional plans, policies, regulations or by the California Department of Fish and Game or U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; c) Have a substantial adverse effect on state or federally protected wetlands (including, but not limited to, marsh, vernal pool, coastal, etc.) through direct removal, filling, hydrological interruption, or other means; d) Interfere substantially with the movement of any native resident or migratory fish or wildlife species or with established native resident or migratory wildlife corridors, or impede the use of native wildlife nursery sites; or e) Conflict with any local policies or ordinances protecting biological resources, such as a tree preservation policy or ordinance? SJMSCP The SJMSCP allows SJMSCP Permittees (San Joaquin Council of Governments; County of San Joaquin; and the cities of Escalon, Lathrop, Lodi, Manteca, Ripon, Stockton, and Tracy) to issue Incidental Take Permits (ITPs) or project applicants to mitigate for impacts to SJMSCP Covered Species resulting from open space land conversion. The ITP allows for the unintentional take of a threatened or endangered species listed under FESA and CESA. The applicant for this Project 4 Environmental Analysis 4.4 Biological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.4-30 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 plans to seek coverage for certain species under the SJMSCP and has been coordinating with SJCOG. Participation in the SJMSCP is voluntary. Should the Project participate, mitigation would be implemented for those species covered by the SJMSCP according to the SJMSCP requirements. Under this approach, EIR mitigation measures would only be implemented for the balance of species impacts identified in the EIR but not covered by the SJMSCP. Project applicants have the four following options to receive coverage, with approval by SJCOG (SJCOG 2000): 1. Pay the appropriate fee. This fee is determined based on which of the four habitats the Project lies within, 2. Dedicate habitat lands as conservation easement or fee title, 3. Purchase mitigation bank credits from a SJMSCP-approved mitigation bank, or 4. Propose an alternative mitigation plan, consistent with the SJMSCP goals. Applicants pay mitigation fees on a per-acre basis to mitigate impacts to various habitat and biological resources. Mitigation is specific to different types of land being impacted. The appropriate fees are collected by the County and remitted to SJCOG for administration. These fees are then used to purchase conservation easements or purchase land for preservation in order to offset Project impacts. This series of low-relief Coast Range Mountains aligns predominately northwest to southeast and separates the Central Valley from the San Francisco Bay Area. 4 Environmental Analysis 4.5 Cultural Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.5-2 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 Specifically, Livermore Valley, followed by the San Francisco Bay, is to the west and San Joaquin Valley is to the east (Farrell and Kitchel 2022). The topography in the vicinity consists of sloping rounded hills with elevations ranging from 380 feet above mean seal level to 509 feet above mean seal level. The basin was historically drained by Mountain House Creek (2 miles north/northwest of the Project) and Patterson Run Creek (1 mile north of the Project), which drains eastward toward the San Joaquin Valley. No perennial or intermittent freshwater sources are located on or adjacent to the Project, although ephemeral streams are present. The deposits within the Project consist of Pliocene to early Pleistocene age Orinda and Oro Loma Formations of alluvial pebble conglomerate, sandstone, and claystone (within the central and eastern portions of the Project site); late Miocene age deposits of the Neroly Formation non-marine, locally pebbly (within the northwestern portion of the site); and surficial sediments of alluvial gravels at the base of the hills (Dibblee 2006). Soils within the Project site consist of the Diablo series, Calla-Carbona series, and Carbona clay loam (NRCS 2022). Prior to water diversions in the nineteenth century for agricultural use and the introduction of nonnative species, the ecoregions adjacent to the Project site (Bay Area and Central Valley basin and adjacent foothills) contained a mosaic of biological diversity (flora and avian, aquatic and terrestrial fauna) that was supported by climatic and hydrological conditions conducive to abundant resource availability and subsistence procurement by aboriginal populations (e.g., Costanoan, Miwok, Yokuts; Preston 1990). Before historic alterations to the landscape occurred, the surrounding environmental setting was characterized by vegetation communities, such as grassland prairies, upland oak-grass savannas, forest, seasonal wetlands, freshwater marshlands and sloughs, and riparian forests along rivers and drainages (Rosenthal et al. 2007). The foothills may have provided a travel corridor to these resources (Farrell and Kitchel 2022). The rolling hills of the Project site appear to have been dominated by annual and perennial native grasses and forbs, with no trees. Native interior grasslands included a variety of grasses and forbs (e.g., California brome, wild rye, lupine, fiddleneck) that would have supported a variety of fauna, such as deer, antelope, rabbits, hares, rodents, and birds (Eviner 2016). Today, the Project is within a rural, agricultural setting with a low population density. The Project site is primarily surrounded by agricultural and undeveloped lands, with limited rural residential to the north and west, the PG&E Tesla Substation to the west, and agricultural land and undeveloped land to the south and east. It is situated in a historically disturbed setting, where the natural habitat has been displaced by non-native vegetation through agricultural activities since the 1870s. Aerial imagery from 1948 depicts a residential ranch complex located immediately northwest of the Project site. Between 1993 and 2005, two residential buildings were constructed along the western Project boundary, and one modular home is located at the northern edge of the Project site, just within the Project boundary. Based on information provided by the parcel landowner, the Project area is annually grazed by cattle. The Project is surrounded by transmission line corridors, the PG&E Tesla Substation to the west, rural residential housing to the west of the Project site and north of Patterson Pass Road, and agricultural fields and wind turbines that dot the surrounding landscape. 4 Environmental Analysis 4.5 Cultural Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.5-3 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 4.5.1.2 Cultural Context The following is a brief overview of the cultural background relevant to the Project site and general vicinity. More detailed descriptions can be found in ethnographic studies, mission records, and major published sources, including Kroeber (1925), Heizer (1978), Moratto (2004), and Milliken et al. (2007). The following cultural context is excerpted from secondary sources, including the Tetra Tech technical report (Farrell and Kitchel 2022) conducted for this Project. Prehistoric Overview Paleo-Indian Period (13,500–10,500 Cal B.P.) During the Holocene, geological events, such as periodic episodes of erosion and deposition, altered, buried, or removed the Late Pleistocene landscape (Rosenthal et al. 2007). Evidence of this period comes from scattered surface locations in the southern portion of the basin. The Paleo-Indian period is characterized by basally thinned and fluted projectile points. The earliest known human presence in the San Joaquin Valley is indicated by artifacts uncovered at the Witt site (CA-KIN-32), located on the remnant south-southwestern shoreline of Tulare Lake. The Witt site has been classified as one of the only known paleontological sites in the central San Joaquin Valley region. During this period, hunters and gatherers crossed very large subsistence areas with extensive foraging ranges (Jones et al. 2003). This is supported by obsidian tracing and dating of projectile points from the Witt site. This evidence indicates that wide-ranging expeditions to distant areas were made for trade or direct procurement of obsidian sources from Napa Valley and those closer to Tulare Lake, but still representing rather lengthy forays east of the Sierra Nevada. During this period, foragers seem to have operated in small mobile groups with low population densities. Archaic Period The period marked by technological and substantial changes in subsistence and material culture is known as the Archaic Period. During this stage, prehistoric residents of the Central Valley developed into efficient hunter-gatherers who successfully exploited localized resource bases. Lower Archaic Period (10,500–7500 Cal B.P.) The environment at the end of the Pleistocene was significantly altered by climate change, which facilitated the production of alluvial fans and flood plains (Rosenthal et al. 2007). The Lower Archaic Period is characterized by isolated finds of stemmed points (similar to Borax Lake, Lake Mojave, Siler Lake, and Pinto wide stem types), stone crescents, and other distinctive, formalized, flaked stone artifacts (Rosenthal et al. 2007). Such artifacts were found further south of the current Project in the Central Valley at the Buena Vista Lake Site (CA KER-116; Fredrickson and Grossman 1977), and the shorelines of Tulare Lake at the Witt site. Faunal remains from the Buena Vista Lake site are limited but diverse, including freshwater fish, waterfowl, freshwater mussels (Margaritifera margaritifera), and artiodactyl bones. North of the Project area, archaeological sites that date to this period have been identified near the Los Vaqueros Reservoir in the hills east of Mount Diablo. Archaeological sites CA-CC0-696 and CA-CCO-637 are about 300 meters apart and both contain artifacts and burials. Charcoal identified under a milling slab at CA-CC0-696 yielded a date of 7920 calendar years before 4 Environmental Analysis 4.5 Cultural Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.5-4 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 present. Archaeobotanical remains found at this site suggest a diet of acorns and wild cucumbers (Wohlgemuth 1997). Middle Archaic Period (7500–2500 Cal B.P.) The Middle Archaic climate was characterized by warmer and drier conditions facilitating the reduction or complete desiccation of Central Valley lakes. Thus, with sea level rising, new wetland habitats were developed and led to the formation of the Sacramento and San Joaquin Delta (Atwater and Belknap 1980; Goman and Wells 2000). This period is categorized by projectile points, such as notched, stemmed, thick-leaf, and narrow concave base darts, groundstone, pottery, twined basketry, basketry awls, and polished stone plummets (Rosenthal et al. 2007). At this time, the classic Windmiller Pattern burial mounds occur. This pattern represents riverine adaptations that were permanent, year-round habitation sites (Rosenthal et al. 2007). Paleobotanical studies of the Windmiller Pattern indicate early use of acorns and pine nuts. Faunal remains include large game animals (elk, deer, pronghorn), leporids, waterfowl, small and large fish, and small rodents. The fauna represented indicates the use of marshes, grasslands, and riverine forests. A component of the Tranquillity site (CA-FRE-48), located near the Fresno Slough (approximately 56 miles north of the Project), radiocarbon dates to this time period. CA-FRE-48 consists of several burials, faunal remains (e.g., Tule Elk, antelope, fox, rabbits [Leporidae]), obsidian and chert lithic tools (e.g., stemmed and notched projectile points), and ground stone (e.g., manos, metates, mortars, and pestles) (Hewes 1946; Moratto 2004). Upper Archaic Period (2500 Cal B.P.–Cal A.D. 1000) During the early portion of this period the environment was cooler and wetter. Populations were characterized by geographically complex sociopolitical organizations as evident from archaeological burial data (e.g., contrasting burial postures), artifact styles, and other items of material culture (Rosenthal et al. 2007:156). Specialized technologies appeared during the Upper Archaic Period, such as bone tools and implements and the production of saucer and saddle-shaped shell beads (Olivella) and ornaments (Haliotis), coiled basketry, and ceremonial obsidian blades. Large amounts of obsidian were obtained from the eastern side of the Sierra Nevada, and lanceolate-shaped bifaces were widely traded (Rosenthal et al. 2007:157). This period was also marked by mortar and pestle use and an increase in plant procurement, specifically acorns (Wohlgemuth 1996; Rosenthal et al. 2007; Rosenthal and Wohlgemuth 2011). Artifact assemblages from the period includes temporally diagnostic forms of beads (Olivella) and ornaments (Haliotis), charm stones (often found cached), cobble mortars, chisel-ended pestles, and dart points. Other diagnostic artifacts include a wide array of bone tools, such as awls, fish spears, saws, and flake tools. During the transition from the Upper Archaic Period to the Emergent Period, the Central Valley experienced drier conditions resulting in resource depression of valley and lowland resources. Native groups abandoned the valley floor and relocated to upland resource areas (Moratto 2004). As the climate improved, people expanded downslope again to the valley floor. 4 Environmental Analysis 4.5 Cultural Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.5-5 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 Emergent Period (Cal A.D. 1000–Historic) The Emergent Period is characterized by the appearance of bow and arrow technology, the rise of wealth-linked social status, the specialization of bead manufacturing, and increased social complexity as indicated by increased variation in burial types and furnishings (Milliken and Bennyhoff 1993; Bennyhoff and Fredrickson 1994; Rosenthal et al. 2007). This period is also marked by the intensification of plant resources, and the use of the mortar and pestle (Wohlgemuth 1996; Rosenthal et al. 2007; Rosenthal and Wohlgemuth 2011). Rosenthal and Wohlgemuth (2011) examined environmental and artifact assemblage data for several upland (west-central Sierra Nevada) and lowland (Central San Joaquin Valley) archaeological sites. The authors suggest that plant intensification was adapted earlier in the lowland regions compared to the uplands due to the greater availability and spatial distribution of various resources in the valley, allowing for more residential stability and increased population. Artifact assemblages are characterized by small corner-notched and side-notched projectile points, Olivella lipped and clam disc beads and bead drills, magnesite cylinders, hopper mortars, pottery, clay balls, and village sites with house pits. Ethnographic Overview The Project area is within the northwestern ancestral land boundaries of the Northern Valley Yokuts, who spoke a branch of the Penutian (Yok-Utian) language family (Gayton 1948; Wallace 1978). The Yok-Utian language is divided into only two distinct subbranches: the Miwok-Costanoan (also known as Ohlone) and Yokuts (Golla 2007). A brief ethnographic summary of the Yokuts culture is provided below. Northern Valley Yokuts The Yokuts fall into three geographical divisions: the Foothill Yokuts, Southern Valley Yokuts, and Northern Valley Yokuts (Gayton 1948; Wallace 1978). The Northern Valley Yokuts’ territory extended southward from between the Mokelumne and Calaveras Rivers to the upper San Joaquin River, and from the crest of the Coastal Range to the west and the Sierra Nevada foothills to the east. The Project site is within the extreme northwestern territory of the Yokuts. The Northern Valley Yokuts generally established villages on low, natural rises along major water courses (i.e., San Joaquin River or its major tributaries) (Wallace 1978). These water sources supported a large variety and abundance of natural floral, aquatic, and faunal resources. The Yokuts practiced a mixed economy of resource procurement and focused on fishing, hunting, fowling, and collecting freshwater shellfish, as well as plant resources, such as roots and seeds (Wallace 1978). Salmon and acorns were important food staples. The basic domestic and economic social unit of the Southern Valley Yokuts was the nuclear family. Additional grouping consisted of patrilineal totemic lineages represented by a totem symbol that was transmitted by father to all his children. Exogamous lineages were formed by families sharing the same totem (Wallace 1978). The Yokuts did not necessarily own land but did practice collective traditional ownership over specific desirable resource areas (e.g., fishing, hunting, seed-grasses, tree groves) among families, and among the tribelet (Gayton 1945:417, 1948:160; Wallace 1978). Individual women could designate a specific tree or seed resource area as their own, and certain areas may have been inherited from one’s mother (Gayton 1945:417). Villages were occupied most of the year until late spring, when families would venture out for several months to collect seed-plant and other resources (Wallace 1978). Collected surplus resources were privately 4 Environmental Analysis 4.5 Cultural Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.5-6 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 owned, especially among women, but were often used in ceremonial reciprocity, gift giving, or trade (Gayton 1930, 1948). The Northern Valley Yokuts were immensely involved in trading resources with neighboring tribes such as the Miwok (to the northeast) and Costanoan (also known as Ohlone, to the west and north). The Miwok traded baskets, bows, and arrows with the Yokuts (Levey 1978). The Costanoan (Ohlone) traded mussels, abalone, dried meat, shells, and salt to the Yokuts, and the Yokuts supplied piñon nuts (Levey 1978:488). Historic Overview In California, the historic era is generally divided into three periods: the Spanish Mission Period (1769–1821), the Mexican Rancho Period (1821–1848), and the American Period (1848– present). These periods began at various times within different parts of the state due to the vastly diverse landscapes Euro-Americans immigrated into, often in areas inhabited by indigenous communities. Spanish Mission Period (1769–1821) The Spanish Mission Period—between 1769 and 1821—designates the time when the Spanish established missions along the California coast (Castillo 1978). The first recorded contact between California natives and Europeans occurred in 1542, when the Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo expedition traveled along the west coast of California (Castillo 1978). Between 1769 and 1833, the Spanish founded 21 missions from San Diego north to the San Francisco Bay area (Presidio). Mission San Francisco Solano (founded 1823), Mission San Rafael Arcángel (founded in 1817), San Francisco de Asís (founded in 1776), Mission San José (founded 1797), and Mission Santa Clara de Asís (founded 1777), were established along the coast near the present-day San Francisco Bay area, over 50 miles northwest, west, and southwest of the Project site (California Missions 2021). Although the inland areas of the San Joaquin Valley were not settled by the Spanish, influences from coastal missions and presidios were felt inland by the end of the eighteenth century. The mission lands extended from the coast east to the San Joaquin Valley. The local Yokuts population was forcibly indoctrinated into the mission system and baptized as neophytes. Many Yokuts were transported to the San José, Santa Clara, Soledad, San Juan Bautista, and San Antonio Missions (Wallace 1978). The padres used the Yokuts as laborers for the mission’s large tracts of land, putting them to work with agricultural and ranching duties. The mental and physical health of the Yokuts people suffered, and many people died or tried to escape to the interior valley (Gifford and Schenck 1926). The padres would send soldiers to search for and retrieve the people who escaped, though many were able to elude the soldiers (Gifford and Schenck 1926; Wallace 1978). The ex-neophytes often led raiding parties targeting the mission cattle herds and horses (Wallace 1978). The transition between the Spanish releases of their northwest coast of California territory to Mexico occurred from 1821 to 1823. Mexican Rancho Period (1821–1848) The period from 1821 to 1848 is referred to as the Mexican Rancho Period (Castillo 1978). In 1821, Mexico gained independence from Spain, and the secularization of the missions was completed in 1834. It was during this period that large tracts of land called “ranchos” were granted by the various Mexican Governors of Alta, California, usually to individuals who had worked in the 4 Environmental Analysis 4.5 Cultural Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.5-7 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 service of the Mexican Government. No Mexican land grants were identified for the Project site. The Rancho Las Positas was west of the Project site in the modern-day town of Livermore (Livermore Heritage Guild 2022). This period is also characterized by declines in the Native American population in the San Joaquin Valley due to the introduction of new diseases and increasing military raids (Wallace 1978). American Period (1848–Present) Following the end of hostilities between Mexico and the United States in January 1847, the United States officially obtained California from Mexico through the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo on February 2, 1848 (Hoover et al. 1962). In 1850, California was accepted into the Union of the United States, primarily due to the population increase created by the Gold Rush of 1849. This increase in foreign immigrants searching for riches and land further decimated the indigenous population. In 1849, Thomas Goodale put up a blue denim tent along Grant Line Road, near Midway Road, which served as a tavern and stagecoach stop for McLead’s Stage Line to Stockton (Wood 1883:462). About 4 years later, Simon Zimmerman purchased Goodale’s tavern and changed the name to Mountain House (Thompson and West 1878:25). Roads to and from Mountain House proceeded north to Martinez (and beyond) and to the south through the Altamont Pass into Livermore Valley. The original route of the transcontinental Lincoln Highway followed Grant Line Road out of Tracy to Altamont Pass. Alameda County was established in 1853 and was carved from parts of Santa Clara and Contra Costa Counties. San Joaquin County was incorporated in 1850. By midcentury, settlers began to move to the area that would become Midway (just west of the Project area). In 1856, Franz (Frank) Haera (a German immigrant) and his wife Cecilia moved to what would become Midway and constructed the Zinc House. In 1872, he was granted 160 acres of land by the United States government (northwest of the Project area) and eventually raised sheep. The 1900 United States Federal Census lists Frank Haera (misspelled “Haira”) as born in Germany in 1832. His occupation is listed as a farmer, his wife is listed as Cecilia (age 45), and a son is listed as Henry (age 6) (U.S. Census Bureau 1900). Frank Haera passed away at 68 years old in Midway, California, in 1901 (The San Francisco Call 1901a). Frank Haera’s 648-acre ranch, livestock (6 horses, 60 head of cattle), 100 tons of hay, and farming implements were auctioned off in November of 1901 (The San Francisco Call 1901b). The Zinc House burnt down in the 1930s (Reeve 2002). The completion of the Central Pacific Railroad (a previously recorded segment, P-39-000098, south of the Project area) in 1869 brought more settlers to the Midway area. The community of Midway began to grow along the railroad and the town eventually included a railroad station, the Midway Public School, a store, a post office (ca. 1870 to 1918), and several residential homes and ranches (Wood 1883; Durham 1998). In 1869, Michael MulQueeney (an Irish immigrant) purchased large tracts of land 2 miles from Midway for ranching. Within 14 years of acquiring land, MulQueeney established one of the largest ranches in Alameda County with 8,000 acres of land and 5,000 to 8,000 sheep (Wood 1883). Michael was married to Mary E., and they had three sons: Michael Jr., John, and William. Michael Sr. passed way in 1884, leaving his ranch and assets to his wife and sons. 4 Environmental Analysis 4.5 Cultural Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.5-8 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 In 1872, Reinhold Haera, a German immigrant and relative of Franz Haera, was granted 160 acres of land near Midway (within the Project area, see Section 4.3). He died in 1926 in Oakland, California (Ancestry 2022). In 1883, Franz and Reinhold Haera and Michael MulQueeney petitioned to construct the Midway Public School. The school was originally built on either the MulQueeney Ranch or Haera Ranch near the intersection of Patterson Pass Road and Midway Road (Shazo 2018). The Midway school house had 16 students in 1878 (Thompson and West 1878:161). The Midway Public School was in use from 1883 to 1946 and the building was eventually moved to the MulQueeney ranch property (1 mile southwest from the Project area) to protect it from vandalism (Shazo 2018). In 1902, John MulQueeney (son of Michael MulQueeney), Cecilia Haera, and Reinhold Haera petitioned the Board of Supervisors to save their homes from the Southern Pacific Company that laid a claim to a right-of-way (ROW) of 400 feet, encompassing the entire town of Midway (The San Francisco Call 1902). By the early 1900s, ranching and farming were the main economic industry in Midway and the rural neighborhood consisted of approximately 30 residents (Shazo 2018). No additional historic information was available for the Haera or MulQueeney families through census sources, historical newspaper articles, or other online sources. The Standard Oil Company constructed an oil pipeline from Bakersfield to the Midway Station in 1910, and the station included several tanks. During this time, the economic use of the land began to shift to include energy production. Electrical power distribution was an important factor in the development of California’s industries and public utilities. The Tesla electrical substation and adjacent Butler Building (P-01-010502) were built during the late 1940s and are west of the Project area. The substation is a critical power source for both the greater Bay Area and San Joaquin County. As of 2018, the substation was connected to the bulk power system via five 500-kilovolt (kV) lines, fourteen 230-kV lines, three 500/230-kV transformers, and two 230/115-kV transformers (PG&E 2018). The Pittsburg-Tesla 230-kV overhead transmission line (P-01-010947) extends 31 miles from the Tesla substation to the Pittsburg substation and is west of the Project. As part of the Pacific Northwest-Pacific Southwest Intertie, high-voltage, electrical transmission lines, the Vaca Dixon-Tesla and Table Mountain Tesla 500-kV, high-voltage, overhead transmission line (P-01-10499) was constructed from the late 1960s to the early 1970s and is west of the Project area. The Tesla-Salado-Mateca 115-kV transmission line (P-10-005337) was constructed in ca. 1920s to 2000s and is southwest of the Project area. 4 Environmental Analysis 4.5 Cultural Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.5-9 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 Wind energy is an important resource for California’s power grid, and wind power generation facilities began to appear in the Project region in the early 1980s. Under the CEQA (Section 15064.5 (a)), a historic resource (e.g. building, structure, or archaeological resource) shall include a resource listed in, or determined to be eligible for listing in, the California Register of Historical Resources (CRHR); or a resource listed in a local register or landmark, identified as significant in a historical resource survey (meeting the requirements of Section 5024.1(g) of the PRC); or any object, building, structure, site, area, place, record, or manuscript that a lead agency determines to be historically significant or significant in the architectural, engineering, scientific, economic, agricultural, educational, social, political, military, or cultural annals of California (Section 15064.5[a]). Under the CCR, Title 14, Chapter 11.5, properties listed on or formally determined to be eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) are automatically eligible for listing in the CRHR. A resource is generally considered to be historically significant under the CEQA if it meets the following criteria for listing in the CRHR (PRC SS5024.1, Title 14; CCR, Section 4852): A. Associated with events that have made a significant contribution to the broad patterns of local or regional history or the cultural heritage of California or the United States (Criterion 1). B. Associated with the lives of persons important to local, California, or national history (Criterion 2). C. Embodies the distinctive characteristics of a type, period, region, or method of construction or represents the work of a master or possesses high artistic values (Criterion 3). D. Has yielded, or has the potential to yield, information important to the prehistory or history of the local area, California, or the nation (Criterion 4). 4 Environmental Analysis 4.5 Cultural Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.5-10 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 Under PRC Section 21074, tribal cultural resources are: 1. California Native American Historical, Cultural, and Sacred Sites Act The California Native American Historical, Cultural, and Sacred Sites Act (the Act) applies to both state and private lands. The Act requires that, upon discovery of human remains, construction or excavation activity must cease and the county coroner be notified. If the remains are Native American, the coroner must notify the NAHC. The NAHC will then identify and notify a most likely descendant. When analyzing cumulative impacts to cultural resources, an assessment is made of impacts on individual resources as well as the inventory of cultural resources within the cumulative impact analysis area. The cumulative area for cultural resources is the Project area and the Altamont Hills area. The Phase 1 heavy-duty truck standards apply to combination tractors, heavy-duty pickup trucks and vans, and vocational vehicles for model years 2014 through 2018 and result in a reduction in fuel consumption from 6 to 23 percent over the 2010 baseline, depending on the vehicle type. The USEPA and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration also adopted the Phase 2 heavy-duty truck standards, which cover model years 2021 through 2027 and require the phase-in of a 5 to 25 percent reduction in fuel consumption over the 2017 baseline, depending on the compliance year and vehicle type. The Project site includes the proposed facility and the generation tie (gen-tie) line corridor (including both the Applicant portion and the portion for which Pacific Gas and Electric [PG&E] will be responsible). San Joaquin County (County) received no scoping comments regarding geology, soils, and paleontological resources. 4.7.1 Existing Conditions 4.7.1.1 Regional Geology The Project site, including the gen-tie corridor, is located on the eastern edge of the Coastal Ranges geomorphic province, not far from the boundary with the Great Valley geomorphic province. The Coastal Ranges province includes a number of named mountain ranges, including the Diablo Range east of the San Francisco Bay Area. The Project site and gen-tie corridor are situated on the eastern flank of the Diablo Range, where the topography is rolling hills and the local relief is just over 170 feet from the highest to lowest point. The Great Valley geomorphic province is a mostly intact (i.e., with limited deformation in the central areas), asymmetric structural trough that has been filled with two thick sequences of sediment deposits. These deposits range in age from the Quaternary to the Jurassic period (CGS 2002). The two sequences are the older Mesozoic Great Valley Sequence and the younger Cenozoic Great Valley fill. The Diablo Range portion of the Coastal Ranges province extends from the northern boundary of Contra Costa County to Watsonville in the south, a length of over 80 miles. The topographic features have resulted from the long history of plate movement and collision along the Pacific Coast and subsequent folding and faulting (Bartow 1991). 4.7.1.2 Local Geology The available sources for geologic mapping in the vicinity of the Project location include Dibblee (1980), Wagner et al. (1991), and the general online map provided by the California Geological Survey (CGS) (Jennings et al. 2010). They characterize the local geology as quite complex, resulting from plate movements and mountain building to the west that has resulted in various geologic “assemblages” (large, fault-bounded blocks containing a unique stratigraphic sequence of different rock units). The assemblages are characterized as primarily Tertiary and overlying older sedimentary rocks from the Cretaceous Great Valley sequence. The assemblage identified in the Project area consists of a poorly consolidated silt, sand, and gravel unit (Pliocene age), Neroly Sandstone (a blue sandstone of Miocene age), and Cierbo Sandstone (a light gray to white quartz sandstone of Miocene age). All of these units overlie various siltstones, mudstones, and sandstones (Great Valley members of Cretaceous age). 4 Environmental Analysis 4.7 Geology, Soils, and Paleontological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.7-2 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 In the Project site and gen-tie corridor, the most generic mapping (Jennings et al. 2010) shows the Tertiary and Cretaceous rock units covered by more recent Quaternary sediment (see Figure 4.7-1). Bedrock Geology 4 Environmental Analysis 4.7 Geology, Soils, and Paleontological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.7-6 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 4.7.1.3 Geologic Hazards Seismicity The Alquist-Priolo Earthquake Fault Zoning Act (1972) and the Seismic Hazards Mapping Act (1990) require the State Geologist to delineate regulatory "Zones of Required Investigation" for active faults. It also established a standardized classification of known and mapped faults in California, by their period of activity: • Historic faults (faults considered to be “active” faults because they have evidence of displacement within the last 200 years); • Holocene faults (faults which have evidence of displacement greater than 200 years ago but less than 11,700 years); • Late Quaternary faults (older faults with evidence of displacement between 11,700 years ago and 700,000 years ago); and • Quaternary faults (oldest faults with undifferentiated age of displacement, but presumably more than 700,000 years ago). There are no known Historic or “active” faults within the Project site (CGS 2010) or gen-tie corridor. There are two faults in the area (Greenville and Las Positas) that are identified as Historic, and these are Fault Zones of Required Investigation. However, they are located more than 7 miles west of the Project site. There is one Late Quaternary fault (Midway), which actually traverses the northeast quadrant of the Project site. Finally, there are two Quaternary faults, the Black Butte Fault and the Corral Hollow Fault, located about 3 to 4 miles southwest of the Project site. Only the Greenville and Las Positas fault zones are listed as Alquist-Priolo Earthquake Fault Zones, while the Midway, Corral Hollow, and Black Butte faults, because of their age, are not. Surface Fault Rupture The Project site and gen-tie corridor do not intersect an established Alquist-Priolo Earthquake Fault Zone, as mapped by the State Geologist (Jennings et al. 2010). The nearest fault that has been designated an Earthquake Fault Zone (i.e., there is evidence of surface rupture sometime in the last 11,700 years) is the Greenville fault zone (over 5 miles west-southwest of the Project site). Although there are other mapped faults in the area (including the Midway fault which traverses the Project site), none of these faults show evidence of movement within the last 11,700 years. The U.S. Geological Survey and CGS developed a version of the Uniform California Earthquake Rupture Forecast (UCERF3) model to evaluate the likelihood of surface rupture caused by an earthquake (Field et al. 2014). The UCERF3 results are available in a Google Earth file, showing the probability of an earthquake with a magnitude of 6.7 or greater on the Richter scale for specific faults or fault zones. The model results for the Greenville fault zone suggest the probability is between 1 percent and 8 percent of such an earthquake occurring within the next 30 years. The model also provides results for the Great Valley Fault (roughly equivalent with the Black Butte fault), suggesting a probability of less than 1 percent that a magnitude 6.7 or greater will occur within the next 30 years. Therefore, the probability of surface rupture caused by an earthquake near the Project is low. 4 Environmental Analysis 4.7 Geology, Soils, and Paleontological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.7-7 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 Seismic Ground Shaking Ground shaking occurs due to a seismic event and can cause extensive damage to life and property and may affect areas hundreds of miles away from the earthquake’s epicenter. The extent of the damage varies by event and is determined by several factors, including (but not limited to) magnitude and depth of the earthquake, distance from the epicenter, duration and intensity of the shaking, underlying soil and rock types, and integrity of structures. The San Francisco Bay Area is seismically active, and moderate to severe ground shaking in the region is possible. However, the UCERF3 model results discussed above suggest that the probability of significant ground shaking caused by an earthquake near the Project site is relatively low. Liquefaction Liquefaction occurs during strong seismic shaking in locations with unconsolidated sediments that are saturated with water. This combination of conditions and action can cause the ground to become unstable. During an earthquake, sediments under these conditions can behave like a liquid, potentially causing severe damage to overlying structures. Lateral spreading is a type of landslide that can occur when unconsolidated liquefiable materials break and spread due to the effects of gravity, usually down gentle slopes. Liquefaction-induced lateral spreading is the finite, lateral displacement of gently sloping ground due to pore-pressure buildup or liquefaction in a shallow, underlying deposit during an earthquake. This phenomenon's occurrence depends on many complex factors, including the intensity and duration of ground shaking, the particle-size distribution of the soil, its density, and shallow groundwater presence. The soil parent material in both the Project site and the gen-tie corridor is unconsolidated alluvium, and the soils are all very fine-grained (clays to clay loams) and generally very cohesive. Therefore, the potential for liquefaction is expected to be low. Landslides Landslides occur when rock, soil, and other debris are displaced by gravity. The potential for material to detach and move down slope depends on multiple factors, including the type of soils, soil moisture content, and the steepness of the terrain. The existing land surface at the Project site has rolling hills and moderate topographic relief (approximately 170 feet of elevation difference). There are no mapped landslides on or around the site or the gen-tie route (DOC 2021). Therefore, landslides in the native materials at the Project site do not normally occur. Subsidence Land subsidence is the gradual settling or sudden sinking of the earth’s surface due to subsurface movement of earth materials. Compaction of subsurface water-containing geologic layers is the primary cause of land subsidence. Regional ground subsidence typically is caused by compaction of subsurface geology as a result of petroleum or groundwater withdrawal. Subsidence has been documented in some areas of the San Joaquin Valley as well as the Sacramento/San Joaquin Delta. However, there are no areas of subsidence identified in the Diablo Range, including the vicinity of the Project site and gen-tie corridor (USGS 2022). 4 Environmental Analysis 4.7 Geology, Soils, and Paleontological Resources Griffith Energy Storage Project 4.7-8 Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 4.7.1.4 Soils The Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) describes the Project site “bedrock” (i.e. the soil parent material) as alluvium derived from sedimentary rock, sandstone, shale, and siltstone (NRCS 2022), with the key word being “alluvium.” Given this, these soils were presumably developed on unconsolidated Quaternary sediment. They are valuable, non-renewable, scientific resources used to document the existence of extinct life forms and to reconstruct the environments in which they lived. Fossils can be used to determine the relative ages of the depositional layers in which they occur and of the geologic events that created those deposits. The age, abundance, and distribution of fossils depend on the geologic formation in which they occur and the topography of the area in which they are exposed. The geologic environments within which plants or animals became fossilized usually were quite different from the present environments in which the geologic formations exist. A preliminary paleontological review was made of published geologic maps, literature, and aerial imagery relevant to the Project site and gen-tie corridor. In addition, a search was performed by University of California Museum of Paleontology (UCMP) personnel to identify previous fossil finds near the Project area using their fossil locality database (Holroyd 2022). Results of this preliminary review indicate strong potential for fossil discovery on and in the vicinity of the Project site and gen-tie corridor. All of the UCMP discovery localities were along a northwest-to-southeast trending line that parallels the Delta Mendota Canal, California Aqueduct, or Interstate Highway 580. The closest location to the Project site is more than 1 mile to the northeast, but fossils were found in the Neroly Formation at two locations, which is also present on the Project site. 4.7.2 Regulatory Setting 4.7.2.1 Federal Earthquake Hazards Reduction Act The U.S. Congress passed the Earthquake Hazards Reduction Act in 1977 to address risks to life and property from future earthquakes through the establishment and maintenance of an earthquake hazards reduction program. (Less than Significant Impact) The Project site and gen-tie corridor do not lie within any mapped earthquake fault zones according to available data. Although the area could be affected by earthquakes or seismic ground shaking, no current data indicate that active (Historic) faults are present within the Project site or gen-tie corridor. The closest earthquake fault is the Midway fault , which bisects the Project site from the northwest to the southeast. However, it is classified as a Late Quaternary fault, with last activity more than 11,700 years ago and less than 700,000 years ago. In addition, the Black Butte fault and the Carnegie-Corral fault zone are located 3 to 4 miles southwest of the Project site. None of these faults/fault zones show signs of recent (Holocene) activity. The Greenville and Las Positas fault zones are the closest active tectonic areas identified as Alquist-Priolo Fault Zones, but they are more than 7 miles west of the Project site. Further, the Project will not include habitable structures and will only have personnel on-site periodically. Therefore, the facility will not potentially expose people or structures to substantial adverse effects associated with rupture of a known earthquake fault. There would be no impact related to surface fault rupture during the construction, operations, or decommissioning periods of the Project. Because the Project facilities potentially could be subject to moderate to severe seismic ground shaking due to the proximity to these fault zones, damage could occur and injuries are possible if personnel happen to be on-site at the time of a significant earthquake. Should strong seismic ground shaking occur at or near the Project site, the on-site facilities could be damaged. However, the Project will be subject to the seismic design criteria of the CBC, which requires that all improvements be constructed to withstand any anticipated ground shaking from regional fault sources and require that the Project owner retain a licensed geotechnical engineer to design the Project components to withstand probable, seismically induced ground shaking.
