Biological Resources Evaluation Report Griffith Energy Project Tetra Tech, Inc 6-1 July 2023 6 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS The Project site is within the planning area for both the San Joaquin County Multi-Species Habitat Conservation and Open Space Plan (SJMSCP) and East Alameda County Conservation Strategy (EACCS). The SJMSCP plan area covers all of San Joaquin County except for federally owned lands. A majority (approximately 90%) of the Project site is within the SJMSCP plan area along the western boundary of San Joaquin County. The current Project site plans avoid Alameda County with the exception of the gen-tie line and access road. The eastern boundary of the EACCS plan area follows the Alameda County line. A small portion (approximately 10%) of the Project site is within the EACCS plan area along the eastern boundary of Alameda County. Additional coordination with the agencies (e.g., CDFW, San Joaquin and Alameda Counties) is recommended to determine if both the SJMSCP and EACCS apply to the Project site or if only one would be used. The SJMSCP (San Joaquin County 2000) and EACCS (ICF International 2010) provide measures to avoid, minimize, and mitigate impacts on special-status species and sensitive habitats. Both of these plans have been finalized. Projects with anticipated impacts to special-status species that are within San Joaquin County are eligible for incidental take coverage under the SJMSCP and would not require incidental take permits for SJMSCP Covered Species. Conversely, the EACCS is a regional conservation strategy that only provides guidelines and recommended avoidance, minimization, and mitigation measures for focal species and habitats. The EACCS does not provide incidental take permits for special-status species, as is the case in a Habitat Conservation Plan such as the SJMSCP, but rather serves as guidance for project-level permits. Therefore, work within Alameda County would still require project-level incidental take permits if impacts to special-status species are anticipated. Recommendations from the SJMSCP and EACCS have been incorporated into Section 6.1. All recommendations within this report are preliminary and will be refined during the CEQA process as more details about the Project design and schedule are determined. 6.1 Additional Survey Recommendations 6.1.1 Rare Plants Two rare plants have the potential to occur on the Project site. Therefore, rare plant surveys are recommended within the Project site. To capture the blooming period for all potential rare plants that could occur, two rare plant surveys are recommended. The first rare plant survey should be conducted in March to April and the second in July to November. The following rare plant species with medium or high potential to occur will be surveyed for during each rare plant survey: • First Rare Plant Survey (March to April): caper-fruited tropidocarpum (Tropidocarpum capparideum). • Second Rare Plant Survey (July to November): big tarplant (Blepharizonia plumosa). 6.1.2 California Tiger Salamander The Project is not within Critical Habitat of CTS or within 5 miles of an area designated as Critical Habitat (USFWS ECOS 2021). Project applicants have the following two options for CTS (ICF International 2010): 1. Assume CTS presence and mitigate. Mitigation would likely entail habitat enhancement/conservation easement on a protected property since there are no agency-approved mitigation banks in the area. Biological Resources Evaluation Report Griffith Energy Project Tetra Tech, Inc 6-2 July 2023 2. Have a USFWS and CDFW-approved biologist conduct surveys using the 2003 Interim Guidance to determine if CTS are present (USFWS 2003). If CTS are present, the project would proceed with avoidance, minimization, and mitigation measures. If no CTS are present, then no mitigation is necessary, but avoidance and minimization measures may still be required by the agencies since suitable upland habitat is present. Therefore, it is recommended to assume presence of CTS and mitigate rather than conducting protocol surveys. No CTS were found during the general biological survey; however, CTS would be overwintering in small mammal burrows at the time of the survey. The Project site contains suitable habitat for CTS and is within the CTS distributional range. If presence is not assumed, to determine the presence/absence of this species on the Project site, a protocol survey would be required (USFWS 2003). A CTS site assessment would be submitted to the USFWS. Upon reviewing the results from the site assessment, USFWS is likely to determine that the Project site contains upland habitat only. At sites that only contain upland habitat and at least one potential breeding pool within 1.24 miles, a one-year drift fence study would be required in the fall and winter, between two consecutive seasons of aquatic larval surveys, to support a negative finding. 6.1.3 Burrowing Owl The SJMSCP does not specifically require BUOW protocol surveys. As allowed under the SJMSCP, this species may be addressed by implementing pre-construction surveys and avoidance buffers (i.e., 75 meters) during construction if nesting owls are found (San Joaquin County 2000). The EACCS recommends that the CDFW protocol survey is implemented (CDFW 2012). The following summarizes the recommendations and timing for protocol-level BUOW surveys: • BUOW protocol surveys require that 100 percent of a project site and 150-meter buffer be thoroughly surveyed by walking transects spaced no more than 20 meters apart to look for potential suitable burrows. • After the burrow transect survey is completed, four breeding season surveys and census of BUOW must be conducted prior to beginning work activities. Nesting season surveys must be conducted between February 15 and July 15, with the first survey occurring between February 15 and April 15 and the last survey occurring between June 15 and July 15. These surveys occur from two hours before sunset to one hour after or from one hour before to two hours after sunrise. • One winter survey must be conducted between December 1 and January 31 if BUOW are not found during the nesting season survey. After the surveys are completed, a report documenting the methods and results must be submitted to the CDFW. After it is determined which of the two plans applies to the Project, that plan should be followed for BUOW as described above. 6.1.4 Additional Requirements Pre-construction surveys are recommended prior to ground disturbance or vegetation clearance to avoid impacts to special-status species that have potential to occur on the Project site. Pre-construction surveys would occur 7 to 30 days prior to construction activities (e.g. equipment staging, potholing) depending on species. Pre-construction surveys would be needed for CRLF, Swainson’s hawk, nesting birds (including raptors), SJKF, and American badger. Pre-construction surveys for SJKF are recommended to include the use of motion-activated cameras, which would be setup and monitored 14 to 30 days prior to construction activities. The recommended density of camera placement is equal to about two camera stations in an average SJKF home range, or about 1 camera station per 2.9 square kilometers (Westall and Cypher 2017). Griffith Energy, LLC (Griffith Energy) proposes to develop approximately 20 acres of a 132-acre site into a battery energy storage facility. A majority of the Project site is located in San Joaquin County, California and a small western portion of the Project site is located in Alameda County (Figure 1). The Project site of 132 acres was surveyed for rare plants in 2022. Tetra Tech previously conducted a literature search and a general biological survey in January 2022 at the proposed Project site (Tetra Tech 2022). Based on the general biological survey results and the habitats found onsite, an assessment of rare plants that could occur onsite was performed (Tetra Tech 2022). The Biological Resources Evaluation Report recommended conducting rare plant surveys for caper-fruited tropidocarpum (Tropidocarpum capparideum) and big tarplant (Blepharizonia plumosa) based on this assessment (Tetra Tech 2022). Both of these species have a California Rare Plant Rank (CRPR) of 1B.1, which indicates that they are rare, threatened, or endangered in California and elsewhere and are considered seriously threatened in California. One rare plant survey was conducted for caper-fruited tropidocarpum in March 2022 and a second survey was conducted for big tarplant in September 2022. The purpose of this rare plant survey report is to document the methods and results of the rare plant surveys. 1.1 Project Site Location, Ecoregion, and Land Use 1.1.1 Project Site Location The Project site is located along the border of San Joaquin and Alameda Counties in California (Figures 1 and 2). It is generally bound by rolling hills used for wind-energy generation, cattle grazing, and residential housing. The Diablo Mountain Range is between 3 and 5 miles south and west of the Project site. The nearest city is Tracy, California, which is 4.5 miles east of the Project site. Interstate 580 is approximately 1 mile to the northeast and Interstate 205 is approximately 2 miles north of the Project site. The Project site is within Township 2 South, Range 4 East, Section 32 in San Joaquin and Alameda Counties. The Project site is centered at a latitude of 37.710 degrees North and longitude of -121.554 degrees West (in decimal degrees). The Project site is also in the U.S. Geological Survey Midway 7.5-Minute Topographic Quadrangle Map (Figure 3). The Project property consists of two parcels with the following Assessor’s Parcel Numbers: 20910019 (San Joaquin County) and 99B-7885-2 (Alameda County). 1.1.2 Ecoregion The Project site is located within the Great Valley Geomorphic Province, which is a broad, flat, alluvial plain about 50 miles wide and 400 miles long in the central part of California between the Sierra Nevada in the east and the Coast Ranges in the west (Jepson Flora Project [eds.] 2021). The Central Valley is composed of two valleys: 1) the northern and smaller valley, known as the Sacramento Valley, which is drained by the Sacramento River; and 2) the southern and larger valley, known as the San Joaquin Valley, which is drained by the San Joaquin River (California Department of Rare Plant Survey Report Griffith Energy Storage Project 2 July 2023 Conservation, California Geological Survey 2002). The Project site is located within the San Joaquin Valley subregion of the Great Valley (Jepson Flora Project [eds.] 2022). 1.1.3 Land Use Based on historical aerial imagery (Google Earth©), the Project site has consisted of herbaceous vegetation and has been used for grazing since 1985. Three houses were built within the Project site between 1993 and 2003. The topography of the Project site appears unchanged throughout this period and is comprised of four hills with slopes of 25 percent or less. The Project site is annually grazed by cattle and also has three onsite houses with ornamental landscaping. The area of the Project site within San Joaquin County is designated as agriculture and open space land (San Joaquin County Community Development Department 2013), and the portion in Alameda County is designated as an unincorporated, wind-resource area (ICF International 2010). Surrounding land uses consist of agriculture, open space, and developed land. The elevational range of the Project site is approximately 300 to 500 feet above mean sea level. Rare Plant Survey Report Griffith Energy Storage Project 7 July 2023 3.0 SURVEY METHODS A literature review was conducted that included the California Department of Fish and Wildlife California Natural Diversity Database (CNDDB) RareFind 5 online database and the California Native Plant Society online Inventory of Rare and Endangered Plants of California (CDFW 2022). Based on the literature review and general biological survey results, two rare plants were determined to have potential to occur on the Project site: big tarplant and caper-fruited tropidocarpum (CDFW 2022; Tetra Tech 2022). Previous CNDDB records of big tarplant and caper-fruited tropidocarpum are located outside the Project site; big tarplant was previously found approximately 25 feet to the west of the Project site in 2003 and caper-fruited tropidocarpum was found approximately 120 feet to the northwest of the Project site in 1987 (CDFW 2022, CNPS 2021). Caper-fruited tropidocarpum blooms from March to April and big tarplant blooms from July to November. Therefore, two rare plant surveys were conducted on the Project site to capture the blooming periods of the rare plant species with the potential to occur onsite. The first rare plant survey for caper-fruited tropidocarpum was conducted in March 2022. The second rare plant survey for big tarplant was conducted in September 2022. Two biologists surveyed the entire Project site during each survey by walking meandering transects throughout the Project site. Transects were spaced 30 meters apart to ensure 100 percent visual coverage of the Project site. All plant species found onsite were identified and recorded. The surveys were conducted during daylight hours and clear conditions at temperatures of approximately 60-80 degrees Fahrenheit. Any rare plant populations found onsite were mapped using a sub-meter accuracy Global Positioning System unit and individuals were counted. Photographs that were taken during the surveys are provided in Appendix A. Rare Plant Survey Report Griffith Energy Storage Project 8 July 2023 4.0 SURVEY RESULTS The Project site is undeveloped other than three small residential areas. All undeveloped areas of the site consisted of Avena spp. – Bromus spp. herbaceous semi-natural alliance. Cattle were actively grazing the site during the rare plant survey in March 2022. Grazing on the site has greatly reduced the cover of non-native grasses such as slender wild oat (Avena barbata) and bromes (Bromus spp.) as compared to the surrounding non-grazed areas offsite. Most of the site cover was comprised of non-native redstem filaree (Erodium cicutarium) with some small patches of non-native cheeseweed (Malva parviflora), black mustard (Brassica nigra), and greenstem filaree (Erodium moschatum). By September 2022, vegetation cover in undeveloped areas of the site was comprised almost entirely of dead non-native annuals such as filarees and mustards with some sprouts of Russian thistle (Salsola sp.). Non-native olive trees (Olea europaea) and pepper trees (Schinus sp.) and ornamental pine trees (Pinus sp.) were found in residential areas. No sensitive natural communities were found during the rare plant surveys. CNDDB records from 2003 documented an existing offsite population of big tarplant (CRPR 1B.1) approximately 25 feet west of the Project site, across Midway Road (CDFW 2022). This existing offsite population was observed during the September 2022 survey since it occurs directly across from the Project site. Multiple 1.6 meters tall big tarplant and many other shorter big tarplant were observed in this offsite area. Similar to the Project site, this area consisted of Avena spp. – Bromus spp. herbaceous semi-natural alliance, but had higher cover of non-native grasses than the site and less intensive cattle grazing. One rare plant species, big tarplant, was found on the western portion of the Project site during the September 2022 rare plant survey. This species was found onsite in erosional areas where soil was disturbed and supported less herbaceous cover. This species is generally known to occur in grasslands and disturbed areas such as burned areas. Specimens of this plant were sent to Dr. Bruce Baldwin of the Jepson Herbarium at University of California, Berkeley and it was verified to be the rare big tarplant by Dr. Baldwin (Baldwin 2022). Two populations of big tarplant were observed within the Project site. The specific locations and boundaries of these populations are shown in Figure 4. Population 1 consisted of 395 individuals and was 0.09 acres in size. Population 2 consisted of 167 individuals and was 0.15 acres in size. Both populations occurred in ephemeral erosional features that had higher cover of bare soil relative to other areas of the Project site. Although this species can grow to over 1.8 meters tall, individuals on the Project site were stunted, likely due to disturbance by cattle grazing, and were up to 0.6 meters tall. Herbivory by cows was observed on some big tarplant individuals. Yellow star-thistle (Centaurea solstitialis), a species rated “High” by the California Invasive Plant Council (Cal-IPC) was found onsite. Yellow star-thistle was predominantly found along fencelines and in areas with stormwater runoff such as near roads. Species rated High by the Cal-IPC have severe ecological impacts on physical processes, plant and animal communities, and vegetation structure. Their reproductive biology and other attributes are conducive to moderate to high rates of dispersal and establishment, and most are widely distributed ecologically. Rare Plant Survey Results Rare Plant Survey Report Griffith Energy Storage Project 12 July 2023 5.0 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS The rare plant surveys were conducted during the appropriate blooming periods for the rare plants (caper-fruited tropidocarpum and big tarplant) that could potentially occur onsite. One rare plant species, big tarplant (CRPR 1B.1), was found on the Project site during the surveys. In addition, the survey results are sufficient to determine absence of caper-fruited tropidocarpum on the Project site. It is recommended that Project impacts avoid the populations of big tarplant if feasible (Figure 4). While big tarplant is not federally or state listed, impacts to this species must be evaluated in the California Environmental Quality Act document and mitigation measures would be required if it cannot be avoided. The following preliminary measures are recommended for this species: • A qualified biologist will flag a minimum no-disturbance buffer of 10 feet around big tarplant populations in the field, and if feasible, these areas will be avoided during construction. To delineate the areas of avoidance, a pre-construction survey would be required during the blooming period for this species (July to November) during the blooming period that occurs prior to the start of construction. For example, if construction were planned to start in June 2024, the area would be surveyed between July and November 2023 and those results would be used to determine the extent of the population areas. • For big tarplant areas that cannot be avoided, a restoration/enhancement plan for impacts to big tarplant will be prepared. The plan will include the following components as needed: figures showing the restored areas; invasive plant species management procedures; topsoil and/or seed collection and dispersal protocols; maintenance requirements; monitoring and performance standards; and reporting requirements. Temporary impacts (i.e., impacts in areas that would be restored to natural conditions) may be mitigated by salvaging topsoil during ground disturbance, storing the soil onsite and protecting it from weed seed dispersal, and then returning the soil horizon to its original profile to keep seeds at the appropriate soil depth. Permanent impacts (i.e., impacts in areas that would not be restored to natural conditions) may be mitigated by enhancing other big tarplant habitat within or outside the Project site, through seed collection and planting and invasive plant control. Topsoil would not be salvaged in the case of permanent impacts, and other habitat enhancement methods would be used, such as seed collection and dispersal, in other non-impacted locations. The actual areas impacted will be mapped post-construction to quantify the amount of big tarplant impacted. Comments from MIG, Inc. (MIG), San Joaquin County’s third-party reviewer of the Draft Environmental Impact Report (EIR), were received on May 19, 2023 and July 21, 2023. Multiple comments on the Biological Resources section of the Draft EIR referenced the presence of an ephemeral pond in the southwest portion of the Project property after a historically high rainfall year. The purpose of the site visit was to document current conditions at the Project site to inform the applicant’s response to MIG’s comments. A detailed impacts analysis will be performed in the EIR. 2.0 METHODS One biologist visited the Project site on June 7, 2023. The following bullets outline the tasks that were performed during the site visit: • Map and assess ephemeral pond in southeast portion of property. Assess habitat in this area for western spadefoot (Spea hammondii), longhorn fairy shrimp (Branchinecta longiantenna), vernal pool fairy shrimp (Branchinecta lynchi), California tiger salamander (Ambystoma californiense, CTS), and California red-legged frog (Rana draytonii). Conduct a jurisdictional delineation. • Evaluate offsite location where West Patterson Pass Road passes under the railroad and assess for potential barriers to CTS wildlife movement. • Check standing water location west of Midway Road for potential to support vernal pool invertebrates. • Map shallow ditch that runs along the southern side of West Patterson Pass Road within 150-meter buffer. The biologist recorded notes, mapped locations on a tablet synced with a global positioning system (GPS) and took photographs. Memorandum 2 July 2023 3.0 RESULTS 3.1 Ephemeral Pond The ephemeral pond was observed in the southeast portion of the property (Figure 1 in Attachment A). The pond appeared to have recently receded, based on the presence of surface soil cracks, but standing water was still present at a depth of approximately 1 to 2 feet deep. The water was turbid and murky, and the soil was a silty clay color of 10YR 3/1. Deep soil cracks were present where the water had receded. Cattle tracks surrounded the pond; cattle were observed elsewhere within the Project property during the site visit. Two debris piles containing cut wood were observed; one is located next to the pond, and one was located in the pond (the general location is shown in Figure 1). Two species of common amphibians were observed to be inhabiting the pond and directly adjacent area, specifically: California toad (Anaxyrus boreas halophilus) and Sierran treefrog (Pseudacris sierra). No tadpoles or fairy shrimp were observed in the water. Photographs of the ephemeral pond are included in Attachment B. 3.1.1 Special-status Species The pond was evaluated for its potential to support special-status species, such as CTS, western spadefoot, and vernal pool invertebrates such as the longhorn fairy shrimp and vernal pool fairy shrimp. If water is present, the ephemeral pond has the potential to support breeding habitat for the CTS and western spadefoot. The pond would not support breeding California red-legged frog due to the lack of emergent vegetation. However, it is infrequently ponded as shown in historic aerial imagery and was not observed during previous Tetra Tech surveys in January, March, and September 2022. This pond is likely only present during high rainfall years, such as the 2022-2023 historically high rainfall year. During a review of available aerial imagery from 1937 to 2022, there was no evidence of ponding water. This pond likely only holds water seasonally during high rainfall years and is typically dry; therefore, the likelihood of longhorn fairy shrimp and vernal pool fairy shrimp presence in this pond is low. Branchiopod cysts can persist in soil substrate for decades, but generally require recurring ponding to continue their lifecycle. The EIR will include an analysis of the Project’s potential impacts to CTS, western spadefoot, California red-legged frog, and vernal pool invertebrates. Measures will be proposed to mitigate Project impacts. Although the ephemeral pond is outside of the Project footprint, it is approximately 40 feet away from the Project footprint boundary and has the potential to be impacted by indirect effects. 3.1.2 Jurisdictional Delineation The pond was evaluated for hydrophytic vegetation, hydric soils, and wetland hydrology per the Interim Regional Supplement to the Corps of Engineering Wetland Delineation Manual: Arid West Region (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers [USACE] 2008), a supplement to the Corps of Engineers Wetland Delineation Manual (Environmental Laboratory 1987), to determine the presence or absence of wetlands and Waters of the U.S. that are potentially subject to regulation under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act. This delineation methodology was also used to evaluate potential Waters of the State under Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB) jurisdiction. “Waters of the State” are Memorandum 3 July 2023 defined by the Porter-Cologne Act as “any surface water or groundwater, including saline waters, within the boundaries of the state” (State Water Resources Control Board [SWRCB] 2019). These may include intermittent or ephemeral waters. The ephemeral pond was also assessed for presence of a lake or pool, measured to the top of bank or edge of riparian vegetation, that is subject to California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) jurisdiction under Section 1602 of the Fish and Game Code. The pond is mostly unvegetated, with approximately one percent cover of sprouting doveweed (Croton setigerus) and black mustard (Brassica nigra) along the edges. No wetland vegetation was observed. Vegetation on the adjacent, gradual slopes next to the ephemeral pond include non-native grasses, such as wall barley (Hordeum murinum), rye grass (Festuca perennis), brome (Bromus spp.), and California burclover (Medicago polymorpha). Wetland hydrology was observed due to the presence of surface water which was approximately 1 to 2 feet deep and surface soil cracks where the surface water has evaporated. Hydric soil was observed due to the presence of redox dark surface (F6) and redox depressions (F8) in each surface layer (0 to 2 inches; 2 to 6 inches; and 6 to 15 inches). The soil was primarily clay/loam with 10 YR, v4/c1 and 10 YR, v3/c1 coloration. The ephemeral pond is not a USACE wetlands due to the lack of hydrophytic vegetation. This feature is not a Waters of the U.S. because it is hydrologically isolated. However, it is likely jurisdictional to the RWQCB and CDFW. 3.2 Railroad Underpass Along West Patterson Pass Road There is a 20-foot-long paved road under the railroad tracks bridge (Attachment B). There are steep dirt berms on the east and wide side of the road. Consistent vehicle traffic was noted along the road. CTS may be able to climb the dirt berm, cross the paved road with vehicle traffic, then use the road under the railroad tracks bridge to access nearby grassland areas. Therefore, the Union Pacific railroad is not a complete barrier to CTS migration, but rather is a partial barrier. 3.3 Standing Water West of Midway Road The standing water observed west of Midway Road within 150-meters of the site has the potential to support vernal pool invertebrates. Aerial imagery indicates that this feature holds water regularly, although ephemerally. However, no standing water was observed in this feature during June 2023, which may indicate that standing water is not present long enough for the entire vernal pool invertebrate lifecycle. Regardless, this area is outside of the Project footprint on the opposite of a paved roadway and will not be impacted directly or indirectly by proposed activities. 3.4 Ditch South of West Patterson Pass Road A shallow ditch that is located on the south side of West Patterson Pass Road within the 150-meter buffer was observed by Tetra Tech during 2022 surveys and by MIG during their April 2023 site visit. This ditch was mapped by Tetra Tech during the June 2023 site visit and has been added to Figure 1 in Attachment A. This ditch ranges from 1 to 8 feet wide and was mostly dry, except for standing water observed at one location north of the railroad and next to the road near the end of the feature. The Memorandum 4 July 2023 ditch is mostly unvegetated with edges of non-native grasses, including brome, slender wild oat (Avena barbata), rye grass, and wall barley as well as yellow star-thistle (Centaurea solstitialis), and poison hemlock (Conium maculatum). 3.5 Other Special-status Species with Potential to Occur 3.5.1 Crotch’s Bumble Bee Crotch’s bumble bee is a candidate for listing under the California Endangered Species Act. Although no bumble bees of any species were observed during the site visit or previous Project biological surveys and there are no known occurrences recorded near the Project Property, floral resources (foraging habitat), burrows and crevices (nesting habitat), and leaf litter (overwintering habitat) were observed. However, the site is routinely grazed and trampled by cattle, which likely interferes with the Crotch’s bumble bee habitat requirements and reduces habitat suitability (Xerces Society et al. 2018). 3.5.2 White-tailed Kite The white-tailed kite is a fully protected species by CDFW. Potential white-tailed kite nesting habitat includes trees located adjacent to the Project Property to the north and northwest. Numerous 8 to 10-foot-tall trees of various species in residential areas have the potential to provide nesting habitat. The open grassland within the Project Property provides potential foraging habitat for white-tailed kites. 3.5.3 Grasshopper Sparrow Tetra Tech notes that MIG observed a grasshopper sparrow, a CDFW Species of Special Concern, by sight and sound during their April 2023 site visit. 4.0 CONCLUSION The Project Site design changed after preparation of the Biological Resources Evaluation Report and Rare Plant Survey Report (Tetra Tech 2022a, 2022b). The Draft EIR analyzes potential impacts to biological resources based on the current Project design. Due to the observation of an ephemeral pond in spring 2023 after a historically high rainfall year, additional special-status species, such as western spadefoot and vernal pool invertebrates, have the potential to occur at the Project Property. Although the ephemeral pond will not be directly impacted by proposed Project activities, there is the potential for indirect effects to the pond itself (which may be jurisdictional to RWQCB and CDFW) and the special-status species that may inhabit the pond. Therefore, the EIR has been revised to analyze these potential effects and include mitigation measures. Additional species, including the Crotch’s bumble bee and white-tailed kite, will be discussed in the EIR and their impacts from the proposed Project activities will be analyzed. Measures will be proposed to mitigate potential impacts to these species. Memorandum 5 July 2023 5.0 REFERENCES Environmental Laboratory. 1987. Corps of Engineers Wetlands Delineation Manual. Griffith Energy Storage, LLC (Applicant), is proposing to construct and operate the 400-megawatt Griffith Energy Storage Project to provide reliable and flexible power to the local electrical system. The property which the Project would be built on consists of 106 acres (Property) of land in San Joaquin County, while the site disturbance will be limited to 32 acres. The Project would interconnect at the Tesla Substation immediately adjacent to the site in Alameda County via a 230-kilovolt interconnection generation tie (gen-tie) line. The energy storage facility is anticipated to house lithium-ion batteries totaling 400 megawatts of energy. Project construction would be in 2024 and is anticipated to come online in 2025. 1.1 Project Setting The Property is approximately 0.9 mile southwest of Interstate 580 and approximately 5 miles southwest of the city of Tracy, adjacent to Pacific Gas and Electric’s (PG&E) Tesla Substation, as shown on Figure 1. The Project site is private land zoned as Agricultural General-160 and designated as General Agriculture. The site includes Grazing Land and Farmland of Local Importance, as classified by the California Department of Conservation. 1.2 Acoustical Metrics and Terminology All sounds originate with a source, whether it is a human voice, motor vehicles on a roadway, or a combustion turbine. Energy is required to produce sound and this sound energy is transmitted through the air in the form of sound waves – tiny, quick oscillations of pressure just above and just below atmospheric pressure. These oscillations, or sound pressures, impinge on the ear, creating the sound we hear. A sound source is defined by a sound power level (abbreviated “LW”), which is independent of any external factors. By definition, sound power is the rate at which acoustical energy is radiated outward and is expressed in units of watts. A source sound power level cannot be measured directly. It is calculated from measurements of sound intensity or sound pressure at a given distance from the source outside the acoustic and geometric near-field. A sound pressure level (abbreviated “LP”) is a measure of the sound wave fluctuation at a given receiver location and can be obtained through the use of a microphone or calculated from information about the source sound power level and the surrounding environment. The sound pressure level in decibels (dB) is the logarithm of the ratio of the sound pressure of the source to the reference sound pressure of 20 microPascals (μPa), multiplied by 20. The range of sound pressures that can be detected by a person with normal hearing is very wide, ranging from about 20 μPa for very faint sounds at the threshold of hearing, to nearly 10 million μPa for extremely loud sounds such as a jet during take-off at a distance of 300 feet. Acoustic Terms and Definitions Term Definition Noise Typically defined as unwanted sound. This word adds the subjective response of humans to the physical phenomenon of sound. It is commonly used when negative effects on people are known to occur. Sound Pressure Level (LP) Pressure fluctuations in a medium. Sound pressure is measured in dB referenced to 20 μPa, the approximate threshold of human perception to sound at 1,000 Hz. Sound Power Level (LW) The total acoustic power of a noise source measured in dB referenced to picowatts (one trillionth of a watt). Noise specifications are provided by equipment manufacturers as sound power as it is independent of the environment in which it is located. A sound level meter does not directly measure sound power. Equivalent Sound Level (Leq) The Leq is the continuous equivalent sound level, defined as the single sound pressure level that, if constant over the stated measurement period, would contain the same sound energy as the actual monitored sound that is fluctuating in level over the measurement period. A-Weighted Decibel (dBA) Environmental sound is typically composed of acoustic energy across all frequencies. To compensate for the auditory frequency response of the human ear, an A-weighting filter is commonly used for describing environmental sound levels. Sound levels that are A-weighted are presented as dBA in this report. Unweighted Decibels (dBL) Unweighted sound levels are referred to as linear. Linear decibels are used to determine a sound’s tonality and to engineer solutions to reduce or control noise as techniques are different for low and high frequency noise. Sound levels that are linear are presented as dBL in this report. Propagation and Attenuation Propagation is the decrease in amplitude of an acoustic signal due to geometric spreading losses with increased distance from the source. Additional sound attenuation factors include air absorption, terrain effects, sound interaction with the ground, diffraction of sound around objects and topographical features, foliage, and meteorological conditions including wind velocity, temperature, humidity, and atmospheric conditions. Acoustical Analysis Report Griffith Energy Storage Project 4 August 2023 1.3 Vibration Metrics and Terminology Vibration is an oscillatory motion that is described in terms of displacement, velocity, or acceleration. Velocity is the most common descriptor used when evaluating human perception or structural damage. Velocity represents the instantaneous speed of movement and more accurately describes the response of humans, buildings, and equipment to vibrations. Peak-Particle-Velocity (PPV) and root mean square velocity are typical metrics used to describe vibration levels in units of inches per second in the United States. However, to evaluate annoyance to humans, the vibration dB (VdB) notation is commonly used. The decibel notation acts to compress the range of numbers required to describe vibration. In the United States, the accepted velocity reference for converting to dB is 1x10-6 inches per second. The abbreviation “VdB” is used for vibration dB to reduce the potential for confusion with sound decibels. In contrast to airborne noise, ground-borne vibration is not an everyday occurrence for humans. The background vibration velocity levels within residential areas are usually 50 VdB or lower, which is well below the human perception threshold of approximately 65 VdB. However, human response to vibration is not usually significant unless the vibration exceeds 70 VdB. For a significant impact to occur, vibration levels must exceed 72 VdB during frequent events, 75 VdB for occasional events, and 80 VdB during infrequent events (Federal Transit Administration 2006). Outdoor sources that generate perceptible ground-borne vibrations are typically construction equipment, steel-wheeled trains, and traffic on rough roadways. Effects of noise at various levels can include interference with sleep, concentration, and communication, and can cause physiological and psychological stress and hearing loss. The USEPA methodology distinguishes between type of construction and construction stage. The basic model assumed spherical wave divergence from a point source located at the center of the Project site to each receptor structure. Furthermore, the model conservatively assumed that all pieces of construction equipment associated with an activity would operate simultaneously for the duration of that activity. An additional level of conservatism was built into the construction noise model by excluding potential shielding effects due to intervening structures and buildings along the propagation path from the site to receiver locations such as residential buildings. 4.2 Projected Noise Levels During Construction The construction processes are anticipated to occur during a period of approximately 15 months and begin in 2024. An industry standard, Cadna-A® was developed by DataKustik GmbH to provide an estimate of sound levels at distances from sources of known emission. It is used by acousticians and acoustic engineers due to the capability to accurately describe noise emission and propagation from complex facilities consisting of various equipment types like the Project and in most cases, yields conservative results of operational noise levels in the surrounding community. The current ISO standard for outdoor sound propagation, ISO 9613 Part 2 – “Attenuation of Sound during Propagation Outdoors,” was used within Cadna-A (ISO 1996). The method described in this standard calculates sound attenuation under weather conditions that are favorable for sound propagation, such as for downwind propagation or atmospheric inversion, conditions which are typically considered worst-case. The calculation of sound propagation from source to receiver locations consists of full octave band sound frequency algorithms, which incorporate the following physical effects: • Geometric spreading wave divergence; • Reflection from surfaces; • Atmospheric absorption at 10 degrees Celsius and 70 percent relative humidity; • Screening by topography and obstacles; • The effects of terrain features including relative elevations of noise sources; • Sound power levels from stationary and mobile sources; • The locations of noise-sensitive land use types; • Intervening objects including buildings and barrier walls, to the extent included in the design; • Ground effects due to areas of pavement and unpaved ground; • Sound power at multiple frequencies; • Source directivity factors; • Multiple noise sources and source type (point, area, and/or line); and • Averaging predicted sound levels over a given time. Cadna-A allows for three basic types of sound sources to be introduced into the model: point, line, and area sources. Each noise-radiating element was modeled based on its noise emission pattern. Larger dimensional sources such as the transformers were modeled as area sources. This was accomplished by evaluating the additional VMT caused by construction and operations. 2.3.1 Vehicle Miles Traveled The VMT metric is project-based and is implemented to help quantify traffic induced by construction and operations. The VMT metric is used to align effects on traffic with greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. VMT is presented as a time-dependent value, i.e., the number of additional VMT per week during construction and operations, as well as a total VMT value for the entire Project. The California Natural Resources Traffic Impact Study Griffith Energy Storage Project 6 February 2023 Agency adopted changes to the CEQA identifying VMT as “the most appropriate metric to evaluate a project’s transportation impacts…Thus, to achieve the State’s long-term climate goals, California needs to reduce per capita VMT.” The VMT values calculated should be compared to a jurisdictionally determined threshold of significance that ultimately dictates whether a project’s traffic impacts are significant and require mitigation or are a less than significant impact. San Joaquin County has not yet developed a threshold of significance for VMT, so in lieu of that the criteria as stated in the Technical Advisory on Evaluating Transportation Impacts in CEQA (CEQA 2018) would apply: The VMT metric can support the three statutory goals: “the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, the development of multimodal transportation networks, and a diversity of land uses.” (Pub. Resources Code, § 21099, subd. (b)(1)) However, in order for it to promote and support all three, lead agencies should select a significance threshold that aligns with state law on all three. State law concerning the development of multimodal transportation networks and diversity of land uses requires planning for and prioritizing increases in complete streets and infill development but does not mandate a particular depth of implementation that could translate into a particular threshold of significance. Meanwhile, the State has clear quantitative targets for GHG emissions reduction set forth in law and based on scientific consensus, and the depth of VMT reduction needed to achieve those targets has been quantified. Tying VMT thresholds to GHG reduction also supports the two other statutory goals. Therefore, to ensure adequate analysis of transportation impacts, OPR [Office of Planning and Research] recommends using quantitative VMT thresholds linked to GHG reduction targets when methods exist to do so.

Traffic Impact Study Griffith Energy Storage Project 10 February 2023 5.0 CONCLUSIONS 5.1 SIGNIFICANCE OF IMPACTS 5.1.1 Vehicle Miles Traveled As noted in Section 1.3.1, there is no established threshold of significance for VMT in San Joaquin County. Since no quantitative, qualitative, or performance level is identified, the significance of 847,667 additional miles traveled must be evaluated based on the three guidance criteria from the CEQA Technical Advisory, and based on the following CEQA criteria, the Project is a less than significant impact for VMT: Reduction of GHG Emissions. The Project is a battery energy storage system facility and the chief aim of constructing such facilities is to increase local energy storage capacity. This Project would support the state policies necessary to meet the California renewable energy standards. California has proceeded to advance energy storage uses to support the grid, including the passage of AB 2514, as well as the resulting California Public Utilities Commission decision for energy procurement targets for each of the investor-owned utilities. The proposed Project would address the limitations of the electrical grid by the increasing demand for renewable energy. Layering energy storage systems into the energy grid improves grid reliability and makes it more resilient to disturbances and peaks in energy demand. The Project and other energy storage systems are used to supply power during brief disturbances, reduce outages and associated impacts to the community, and substitute for certain large footprint transmission and disruption upgrades. Additionally, Griffith conducted an Air Quality and Greenhouse Gas Technical Report for San Joaquin County which concluded a “less than significant impact” for both construction and operations emissions. The GHG technical report identified a quantitative threshold of significance for GHG emissions. The analysis included in that report accounted for construction traffic emissions to determine the total emissions for the Project. Using this definitive quantitative metric yielded a “less than significant impact.” Based on this conclusion a threshold value for VMT would likely be much higher than the Project generated VMT. This assertion is in line with the fact that the guidance for conducting VMT analysis originated with GHG emissions reduction regulations and goals and the guidance states “OPR recommends using quantitative VMT thresholds linked to GHG reduction targets when methods exist to do so.” Diversity of Land Use. Diversity of land use is a more difficult criteria to quantify for a comparative analysis. According to CEQA (2018), “State law concerning the development of multimodal transportation networks and diversity of land uses requires planning for and prioritizing increases in complete streets and infill development but does not mandate a particular depth of implementation that could translate into a particular threshold of significance.” The Project would diversify land use by changing the current use from undeveloped cropland grazing land to renewable energy storage. While the Project would increase the VMT from undeveloped to developed conditions, nearly all of the VMT are added during a relatively short construction time window. The expected facility maintenance would generate infrequent and light traffic during operations, and it is anticipated that eventually maintenance visits would be reduced to once a month or less and not impact peak hour traffic. Development of the Project would therefore support California’s statutory energy goals—reduction of GHGs through development of a storage facility for renewable energy, development of multimodal transportation networks, and a diversity of land uses. Development of Multimodal Transportation networks. This CEQA guidance criteria is not relevant to the Project. Water Supply Assessment Griffith Energy Storage Project 4 February 2023 1.0 PROJECT DESCRIPTION The Project is a proposed energy storage facility housing lithium-ion batteries totaling 400-megawatts of energy on a 106-acre property of land in San Joaquin County. The Project property is approximately 0.9 miles southwest of Interstate 580 and approximately 5 miles southwest of the City of Tracy, directly east to the Pacific Gas and Electric’s Tesla Substation. The energy storage facility would interconnect at the Tesla Substation immediately adjacent to the site in Alameda County via a 230-kilovolt interconnection generation tie (gen-tie) line. The Project would substantially increase energy storage capacity and address limitations of the electrical energy grid by increasing the efficacy of renewable energy. This Project and other energy storage systems are used to supply power during brief disturbances, reduce outages and associated impacts to the community, and substitute for certain large footprint transmission upgrades. Construction of the Project is anticipated to last approximately 12-months, plus 3 months for commissioning, with an estimated 10,000,000 gallons of non-potable water (approximately 30.7 acre-feet) needed for dust suppression, soil compaction, and other construction related purposes. During the Project operation and maintenance phase, the expected maintenance would generate little worker traffic and no heavy equipment would be utilized during normal operation. No permanent sanitary facilities would be required during operations. Fire protection service is expected to be provided by the Tracy Rural Fire District. The project site is approximately 3 miles west of the Tracy Rural Fire District Fire Station 94. Water Supply Assessment Griffith Energy Storage Project 5 February 2023 2.0 SUPPLY AND DEMAND ANALYSIS The WSA assesses if the demand associated with a project is available. The Project is estimated to require 10,000,000 total gallons of water (30.7 acre-feet) for construction use for a 12-month duration, plus 3 months of Project commissioning. That volume of water is equal to roughly 30 gallons per minute continuously for 12 months of construction use. One existing domestic well is located within the Project site. Per historic boring reports the well is 200 feet deep with the static water level depth at 32 feet. Downhole video surveys and a pumping test will be needed to confirm these values, the condition of the well, and if rehabilitation of the well will be needed prior to use. There is no public water system that provides water to the Project site, but the Project site is adjacent to the City of Tracy which has a public water system. The expectation is that the construction contractor may choose to haul water from the City of Tracy. This analysis includes both groundwater sources as well as public water supply sources from the City of Tracy. 2.1 SAN JOAQUIN RIVER HYDROLOGY REGION (TRACY SUBBASIN) The Project site is located within the Tracy Subbasin (Basin 5-022.15) of the San Joaquin River Hydrologic Region. Per the California Groundwater Update 2020 (Bulletin 118) the San Joaquin River Hydrological Region covers 15,200 square miles in Central California and provides nearly 4 million acre-feet per year of water to the area. The California Department of Water Resources (DWR) has identified the basin as a medium priority basin and therefore requires a Groundwater Sustainability Plan (GSP) pursuant to the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA) (DWR 2019). SGMA requires medium- and high-priority basins to develop groundwater sustainability agencies (GSAs), develop GSPs, and manage groundwater for long-term sustainability. The Tracy Subbasin GSP was finalized in 2021 (GEI 2021) and will be updated every 5 years as additional information for the subbasin becomes available. The GSP identifies sustainability indicators for the subbasin, defines significant and undesirable results, minimum thresholds, and measures objectives that will be used to guide and define sustainable conditions and overall groundwater management goals within a 20-year period (GEI 2021). The GSP describes the six agencies throughout the subbasin (GSAs) that are responsible for sustainably managing groundwater in the subbasin, with each GSA having jurisdiction within their respective areas. Key components for defining sustainable conditions include water quality and groundwater level monitoring and monitoring of land subsidence via satellite-based-radar measurements. The GSP also provides technical information used to develop water budgets under historical and current conditions and under future use conditions with climate change consideration. The water budgets were developed using a state- developed model for the entire Central Valley. The water budgets show a surplus for the historic conditions and a deficit for future conditions with climate change. The GSP presents management actions for the subbasin to resolve deficits predicted by the model-based future groundwater budget. The management actions include one project that can resolve the deficit that includes reducing groundwater pumping by 1,000 AFY. There are also two supplemental projects: one project that benefits the Upper aquifer by reducing pumping by up to 3,000 acre-feet per year (AFY) and a second project that can increase recharge to the Lower aquifer by up to 3,000 AFY (GEI 2021).
